Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to speak to Bill C-81 , the accessible Canada act, introduced in the House by the Minister of Sport and Persons with Disabilities on March 20. This legislation is a crucial step toward making Canada a more accessible and inclusive country for all Canadians, particularly those with disabilities.
The Government of Canada is committed to an accessible Canada for all, no matter their abilities, and the accessible Canada act is an important part of this commitment. This bill is designed to address the gap in the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act that is currently in place for other provinces and territories.
The bill will establish a comprehensive accessibility law for Canada. It will provide clear accessibility requirements for federal institutions, including the federal public service, the Canada Revenue Agency, the RCMP, and all federal Crown corporations, such as the CBC, VIA Rail, and the Bank of Canada.
The bill will set out five key accessibility requirements: preventative measures; standards for goods, services, facilities, and buildings; standards for the provision of information and communications; employment standards; and transport standards.
The bill will create a new office of the accessible Canada chief commissioner that will be responsible for administering the act and working with the public service and the minister to achieve accessibility objectives. The office will also oversee a new accessibility standards development organization, which will be responsible for the development of accessibility standards in consultation with persons with disabilities.
The bill will also create a new position of accessible Canada commissioner that will be responsible for promoting compliance with the act and conducting investigations in response to complaints.
The bill will create a new disability prevention fund of $15 million per year, beginning in 2019-20

The Bill is a significant step towards achieving a fairer and more equitable trading relationship between Ireland and developing countries, a relationship that is based on a common understanding of justice and human rights.
In some respects, the Bill is a response to the international context in which we find ourselves. The context is one of growing inequality and injustice in the world, particularly in the developing countries. The growing disparity between rich and poor countries, and the failure of the international trade system to address this, are issues of concern to the international community. The current crisis of global capitalism is also one of the main contributors to this situation. The Bill is also a response to the need for greater regulation in our trading practices and a response to our own self-interest, given the damage done to our reputation as a result of our record on trade justice.
The Bill has four main components. First, it seeks to establish the Irish Trade Justice Forum. This is a voluntary forum that would bring together a range of stakeholders with an interest in trade issues. These stakeholders would include the Government, the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, development agencies, nongovernmental organisations, the farming and fishing communities, business and industry. It would, in effect, be the Irish civil society counterpart to the WTO trade policy review mechanism. The Bill makes provision for the forum to undertake its own review of Ireland's trade policy every two years. This review would be published and discussed at a public forum. A report would be presented to the Oireachtas, as well as to the Government. The forum would also be able to monitor Ireland's implementation of relevant international trade agreements and international trade standards.

We have seen a steady increase in the number of people seeking emergency accommodation, with 7,300 homeless in the first quarter of 2018 and a total of 10,363 people in emergency accommodation last month. That figure includes 2,700 children, 600 of whom are in emergency accommodation with their mothers. When we talk about the numbers of people on the housing waiting list and those in emergency accommodation, it is very important to remember those who are without the luxury of accommodation and are sleeping rough. The Government has a moral responsibility to ensure that everyone is housed and the Minister is not doing nearly enough to provide for those in need. The number of people sleeping rough increased by 15% in the first three months of this year and the latest figures from the Dublin Region Homeless Executive indicate the number of rough sleepers in the capital alone increased by 31% in the first quarter of 2018. The numbers do not include the many others who are not in emergency accommodation but are at risk of becoming homeless, such as those who are couch surfing or sleeping on the floor in shared accommodation.
There has been a 50% increase in the number of families in emergency accommodation in the last year alone and 80% of the people in emergency accommodation in Dublin are from the southside of the city. While it is good to see the Government finally starting to move on some of the measures, it is not enough. The Government needs to commit to building 20,000 social houses every year and to give the Minister for Housing, Planning and Local Government, Deputy Eoghan Murphy, the resources he needs to get the job done.

Minister for Planning Richard Wynne today announced the state's population is expected to grow by 1.2 million by 2051, with more than 1.2 million new dwellings needed across Victoria to accommodate this growth.
Under the Victorian Planning System, a residential development must have a planning permit in order to commence construction and be occupied. While the number of new homes being built is steadily increasing, Victoria's planning system is also becoming more efficient.
In the last 12 months, more than 1,300 planning scheme amendments were approved, with more than 90% of permits being approved within 60 days. New homes are also being delivered in areas with public transport, services and community facilities, reducing the need for people to drive.
The Andrews Labor Government is working to ensure Victoria's planning system is fit for purpose by investing $10 million to deliver the new Victorian Planning Authority, the first step in creating a single strategic planning agency.
The Government will invest a further $6.9 million over three years to support the new Victorian Planning Authority, with the agency to work with councils and communities to create better plans that reflect local needs and aspirations.
The Victorian Planning Authority will also be responsible for the Melbourne Metropolitan Planning Strategy to ensure that Melbourne's growth is managed for current and future generations.
"We're building more new homes than ever before, and there's more to come - with thousands of new jobs to be created under the new Victorian Planning Authority."

The Labour Party is committed to building the homes that we need to create a nation of home owners. It is a policy that we fought the election on, and it is a policy that we will fight the next election on.
In 2015, the average house price was £190,000. Today it is £231,000. In the last year alone, house prices have increased by £30,000. At the same time, wages have stagnated. The average wage is £28,200. That is £2,000 less than it was in 2010.
Labour will build 100,000 homes a year on top of the number that are currently being built. That will be the biggest house building programme since the 1970s. Our ambition is to build 200,000 homes a year in total.
The problem is that in too many parts of the country there is not enough land available. As the Institute for Public Policy Research has shown, since 2000 land prices have increased by more than the cost of construction. That is why the Conservatives have failed to build the number of homes that we need.
If we want to build the number of homes that we need, we need to change the law. We need to change the system of planning so that it works for local people, not against them.
First, the law should be changed so that, in areas where there is a shortage of housing, the land on which homes are to be built should not be considered to be brownfield unless it has been built on previously. In these areas, every piece of brownfield land should be available for development, and the community should have a say in what is built.
Secondly, it should be easier for people to build their own homes. That is why we will support co-operative development trusts. We are committed to giving local people a greater say in what is built in their area.
Thirdly, the planning process should be simple and fast

Madeleine began her career in 1924 as a nurse in the United States, where she specialized in surgical nursing. When she returned to Canada, she worked in Saskatchewan and then British Columbia, where she settled in 1937 to work as a nurse in a mission hospital in the Shuswap region.
She became friends with members of the Shuswap band, including Chief Peter Kelly, who was elected to the House of Commons in 1949. She and Kelly were married in 1947.
Madeleine was the founder of the Salmon Arm Museum of Technology. She was instrumental in the design and development of the museum, which opened in 1971, and served as curator and president of the society until her death in 1976.
Madeleine was an advocate for the disabled. She initiated many programs for people with disabilities and helped establish the first organization for the disabled in the Shuswap region.
She received many honours, including the Canadian Centennial Medal in 1967 and the Order of Canada in 1974.
A street in Salmon Arm was named in her honour and a commemorative plaque was erected at the Salmon Arm Museum of Technology in 2007. She is truly an inspiration to all of us.

The 30th anniversary of the Falklands Conflict is an opportunity to reflect on that conflict and its aftermath. The families of those who were killed, the veterans who served and the people of the Falklands and of Argentina have all been affected by it in different ways.
In 1982, this country stood with the people of the Falkland Islands and we will never forget that. It is right that we remember those who were killed and acknowledge their service in a dignified and solemn manner. This debate gives us the opportunity to do that.
It is also an opportunity to recognise the role of the armed forces, especially those who served in the Falklands. I say that as someone who did not serve in the Falklands but who served with some of the veterans of that conflict when I was in the Royal Navy. The conflict was one of the defining moments of our armed forces’ history.
There were 5,800 service personnel involved in the conflict, and 1,000 were wounded. Many of those wounded are still coping with the effects of their injuries. Others are still living with the physical and mental effects of their service. The Ministry of Defence has taken a long-term approach to those who served in the Falklands.
A new veterans’ welfare unit was set up in 2002 to provide a single point of contact for all veterans’ welfare issues. In 2005, the Falklands veterans’ badge was created to acknowledge the contribution of the veterans and their families and to ensure that they received all the benefits they were entitled to. The badge is issued to all personnel who served in the Falklands between 2 April and 20 June 1982, and is available to the families of those who were killed. The badge is a small but significant gesture of our recognition and gratitude to the veterans and their families.

I am pleased to rise to speak today to Bill C-77, an act to amend the National Defence Act and to make consequential amendments to other acts. It is the last act in a three-part series of bills that are aimed at ensuring that the justice system in Canada's military is up to date and consistent with our current understanding of human rights.
Last year, my colleague, the member for Winnipeg North , spoke to Bill C-15, which amended the National Defence Act by removing any reference to homosexuality, including homosexuality as an offence under the code of military justice. Bill C-77 continues this important work by addressing many of the issues that my colleague referred to in his speech.
It is important to remind ourselves that the National Defence Act was drafted in 1985 and it is long overdue for an update. The Canadian Armed Forces are no longer a conscripted military, but an all-volunteer force. The military justice system should reflect that fundamental change.
I will focus on a few issues with Bill C-77. First, we welcome the bill's intention to modernize the treatment of sexual offences. These are serious issues that have become front and centre for Canadians. I think of the many stories in the media of women who have been sexually assaulted and who, at times, are afraid to speak out because they believe that no one will believe them. This is exactly why we need to modernize the National Defence Act to ensure that the Canadian military justice system is consistent with civilian courts, and that military judges and juries are given the necessary tools to address these very serious issues.
As well, the NDP welcomes the intention to increase the maximum sentence for murder from life imprisonment to a maximum of 90 years, and to remove a provision in the code that automatically discharges a person from service upon conviction of murder. It is vital that we do all we can to reduce the stigma around dementia and encourage people to be open and honest about their concerns. Essentially, in the course of the judicial review proceedings, the Government have been asked to provide copies of witness statements that the then Secretary of State made to the High Court in the course of the judicial review proceedings. The Government have not provided those witness statements. They have instead provided summaries of the witness statements and copies of the written submissions. There are good reasons for that. If the witness statements were to be provided, they would be subject to the provisions of section 17 of the Official Secrets Act 1989, which means that they would be inadmissible in a judicial review. As a result, the court could not do the job it is supposed to do, which is to review the decision-making process of the Secretary of State. It would not be able to review it unless it had the witness statements. If the witness statements were disclosed, the Secretary of State would have to face the court with the evidence against him. In other words, the Secretary of State’s witnesses would be in the witness box, and he would be obliged to cross-examine them in the course of a judicial review.
I am sure we all have experience of judicial reviews. For example, when we take a decision about the use of land or about planning, the law is very clear that if the decision-maker does not follow the proper procedures, his decision will be quashed. I have done that in the past in the High Court. There are numerous instances of the courts quashing decisions by the Secretary of State. The court’s decision is based on the evidence that the Secretary of State places before the court. However, if the court does not have access to the evidence, it is not able to make a determination. It cannot make a determination on the evidence. It is obliged to make it on the Secretary of State’s summary of the evidence. That is why it is so important that the court has access to the evidence

The government’s response to this issue is to give Canadians more money in the form of subsidies and tax cuts. In the case of subsidies, the government is taking money away from other programs, which is further contributing to the deficit. In the case of tax cuts, the government is giving money to Canadians, which is only going to lead to more spending.
The government’s response to the cost of living crisis is to give more money to Canadians and to take money away from other programs. This is a short-term solution, and it is not going to fix the problem.
The cost of living is increasing, and the purchasing power of Canadians is not. The government is spending more money and giving more money to Canadians, but prices are still going up. This is a problem that needs to be addressed, and it needs to be addressed now.

Leader of the House said he had a mandate, and he was right to say that. But if he believes that the mandate is to leave the European Union with a no-deal Brexit, he is wrong. What will the House do next? The Leader of the House has repeatedly said that the House will consider the deal when it returns. Of course, he knows perfectly well that that is not right: the Prime Minister has already made it clear that she will not put the deal back before the House, for her own reasons. We have a Government who have lost their mandate, not just in this House but in the country.
The Government have lost their mandate. The only reason we have not had a general election is that we have the threat of a no-deal Brexit. The only reason that we have not had a general election is that the Prime Minister does not have a majority. The Prime Minister said, “I think it’s important that people understand that a number of factors have come together that have pushed energy prices up.” One of those “factors” is his Government’s decision to end the requirement for energy companies to pay a set price for their carbon emissions. Another is his decision to scrap the energy price cap. Another is his decision to scrap the Green Deal, which would have helped homes to reduce their energy consumption.
Another “factor” is the failure of this Government to create and enforce the energy efficiency standards that were in place before it came to office. If the Government had maintained those standards, we would already be seeing huge reductions in energy consumption and carbon emissions, and so would be well on the way to a future where our energy prices are set by our ability to produce energy from sustainable sources, not by the ability of fossil fuel companies to exploit vulnerable consumers.
The Government could, and should, have been taking action on energy efficiency for the past four years. The Government could, and should, have been acting to provide targeted help for pensioners. But the Government has been too busy planning an energy policy that is reliant on more gas extraction, more fracking, more offshore exploration, and more nuclear power stations, to give any thought to how to ensure that consumers are protected from rising energy prices.
As the Prime Minister has now finally admitted, his energy policy is not only incapable of keeping energy prices low, it is also incapable of bringing the UK to a position where our energy is sourced from sustainable sources, so that energy prices are set by our ability to produce it, not by the ability of fossil fuel companies to exploit vulnerable consumers.

I want to think about those family members and the friends of the family who are left behind to pick up the pieces and deal with this absolutely horrendous situation. I want to think about the impact it will have on the people around them. I want to think about the impact it will have on the community of Tullamore, the people who knew her and who knew her family, and those who knew her in school.
I want to ask people to put themselves in the position of the family and think about what it will be like to be left without their daughter and sister, left without their little girl. I want to think about what it will be like for the family to be without her. I want to think about what it will be like for those who knew her in her school and in the community in Tullamore. Aisling was a young lady who was a talented sportswoman, a musician, a teacher and a lovely young girl. We must put ourselves in the position of the family to think about what it will be like for them in the future. Aisling had everything to live for.

That’s a very good point. And if I’d taken a different path, I might have done things differently. But I didn’t, so I didn’t.
It’s very, very interesting that in some ways it’s easier to look back on one’s own life than to look at someone else’s.
We don’t have to worry about the consequences of our actions because they have already occurred. But we do have to worry about the consequences of what we might do.
But if we were in a world where things could be undone, it would be much easier, wouldn’t it, to change things?
I wouldn’t want to undo anything. The good and the bad is all there together. It’s a bit like, say, a poem.
If I were to go back and change anything in the poem, then I would change everything. The whole poem would be different. There’s no point in saying, ‘This is the bit I want to keep.’ I can’t keep that bit because it only exists as part of the whole.
If I were to go back to the beginning and say, ‘I’m going to keep that bit of the poem and throw the rest away,’ it would be a totally different poem. And that’s what life is like.
So I’m not interested in changing history or changing other people’s lives. I’m interested in learning from history and from other people’s lives. And that’s what I hope the book will do.
I think there are all sorts of things to be learned from looking at the choices that other people make, and the choices they don’t make. And that’s what I’ve tried to do in the book.

The most important principle of sustainability is that we should not take more from the environment than it can replace in a year. This is the meaning of the term ‘ecological footprint’. The concept of ecological footprint is used to describe how much land and water is required to produce the resources that we consume and to absorb our wastes. We can then compare the average footprint of people from different countries to see whether they are living within the limits of what the planet can sustain.
But, we can also compare the average footprint of different generations. The footprint of the average person from the industrialised world is about 1.5 hectares, but the average footprint of people in the developing world is about 0.7 hectares. The footprint of the average person from the industrialised world is about 3 times as large as that of the average person from the developing world. This means that, over the last 50 years, people from the industrialised world have been consuming at about 3 times the rate that people from the developing world can sustain.
The reason for this difference is that, over the last 50 years, people in the industrialised world have been using the resources of the developing world as if they were their own. This is the opposite of sustainability. We cannot use resources at a rate faster than they can be replaced without causing long-term damage to the planet.

The 2022 theme for the Holocaust Memorial Day Trust is ‘One Day’. This theme asks us to reflect on the importance of standing together, and how what happens to one of us affects all of us. I will be visiting my local commemoration event in Redditch this evening, where I will be giving an address.
The Holocaust Memorial Day Trust have also launched an online exhibition, which can be found here.
I am proud that my own family has been involved in the Jewish community and in Holocaust remembrance and education for many generations. My late Grandfather, Maurice Levene, was the Rabbi at the Balsall Heath Synagogue in Birmingham, and was the driving force behind the development of the Holocaust Educational Trust. The Holocaust Educational Trust is a charity that works with schools across the country to educate young people about the Holocaust and to encourage them to challenge all forms of hatred and prejudice. My Aunt, Dr Margaret Levene, was one of the Trust’s founding Trustees, and I was honoured to be asked to take up the baton from her and my late Grandfather by joining the Trustees of the Trust in 2011. I continue to hold the position of Honorary President of the Trust.
During the Covid pandemic, the Holocaust Educational Trust have continued to work with schools across the country to share stories of the Holocaust and of other genocides. They have also published several resources which can be found here.
The Trust are currently working with a group of 25 Holocaust survivors in the UK to gather their testimonies. The Trust hopes that these testimonies will be used in the future to help educate a new generation about the Holocaust, so that we never forget, and can learn from our past. For more information, visit the Trust’s website.

The HSE is not in a position to negotiate a price and is instead reliant on industry providing a price. However, the Department of Health’s Medicines Management team are the only party in a position to negotiate a price. However, they are unable to do so because of the lack of transparency in the HTA process. The HSE and industry are therefore forced to enter into negotiations on a price that the HSE has no means of verifying. This is in stark contrast to the situation in other EU countries, such as the UK, where the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) publishes all of the clinical and cost-effectiveness evidence that they use in order to arrive at a health technology assessment recommendation.
A lack of transparency is evident in the HSE’s own process of health technology assessment. There is no information available on the outcome of the HTA process and how this is used to make a decision. If the HSE were to publish the evidence base for their health technology assessment recommendations this would provide a useful starting point for the negotiations between the HSE and industry. This would allow the HSE and industry to arrive at a fair price for new medicines and this, in turn, would speed up the process of introducing new medicines to the health system.

It was referred to the Joint Committee on Health for pre-legislative scrutiny. The committee report was debated and adopted in the House on 19 July. We are now coming to the final phase of the Bill's passage through the House. However, the Bill is a shambles, as it does not reflect the views of the Minister, as I am about to outline.
The Bill was supposed to be a simple Bill to repeal the minimum pricing legislation. The Bill was never intended to be a Bill to introduce alcohol price increases and it was not supposed to be a Bill to repeal the minimum pricing legislation and allow the Minister to introduce price increases. That was not the original intention. When the Bill was introduced, the Minister of State and her officials said it was to repeal the minimum pricing legislation. However, it now appears it will repeal the minimum pricing legislation and introduce price increases. This is why we have tabled this amendment. When the Bill was introduced, the Minister of State stated that the minimum pricing legislation was to be repealed in order to ensure the country remained competitive with the UK and Northern Ireland. However, the Bill was not amended in that regard. The Bill was introduced to repeal the minimum pricing legislation but now, as we are about to see, it will repeal the minimum pricing legislation and allow the Minister to introduce price increases. It is very difficult to understand how the Minister of State and the Government can be in this position.

On 1 February 1999, I laid before the House and placed in the Library of the House a copy of the 1998 review of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1965 (c. 95) and of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 (c. 38). The review was undertaken by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, the independent body established by the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.
The Dangerous Drugs Act 1965 and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 (the 1965 and 1971 Acts) provide the framework within which the drug laws are administered. The Acts define the controlled drugs and provide for their possession, supply and manufacture to be controlled by way of licensing and for penalties for unlicensed activities.

The IPCC warns that without urgent action we could face a future of climate catastrophes including a rise in sea level of up to 3 metres, widespread ocean acidification and mass extinction of species.
The government must stop ignoring science and take urgent action to phase out fossil fuels. This can only be done by working with our allies and partners across the world to bring together the greatest scientific minds to develop alternative green technologies.
It is therefore vital that the UK has a seat at the table of the next IPCC Assessment report to ensure that the scientific community is prioritised and that all countries are engaged in developing green technology for the benefit of all of humanity.
In my constituency, as in many parts of the UK, there is a desperate need for infrastructure upgrades and improvements. We have a major challenge in the north of the country with the infrastructure we need to meet our commitments on renewable energy. The Green Energy Act 2008 was supposed to make it easier to get planning permission for these projects, but 13 years on, the north is being left behind. We need to stop treating the north as a dumping ground for fossil fuels and stop leaving the north behind when it comes to the green revolution. The UK can become a world leader in clean energy, but we need the right political leadership.
As the government has admitted that its target of net zero by 2050 is unachievable, it is time for Labour to set out a clearer vision for our energy future. That vision must not be based on false promises about nuclear, and it must not be based on uncosted targets. We need an energy policy based on the science of the IPCC and the science of the Committee on Climate Change.

A lithium-ion battery is an electrochemical device that converts chemical energy to electrical energy, and vice versa. This is possible because of the chemical reaction between lithium ions and graphite. These two components are contained in the battery’s two electrodes, the anode and the cathode.
A normal battery functions with the lithium ions moving between the electrodes during discharge and charge. But if this chemical reaction is interrupted, the lithium ions react with other components of the battery and cause a thermal runaway.
In a lithium-ion battery, there are four components: a negative electrode (anode) made of graphite, a positive electrode (cathode) made of nickel-cobalt-aluminum, a separator between the electrodes, and an electrolyte.
The cathode is generally made of nickel-cobalt-aluminum and is the positive electrode where lithium ions are stored when the battery is charging. The negative electrode is made of graphite, and lithium ions move from the cathode to the anode during discharge.
In a lithium-ion battery, the positive electrode is the cathode. It’s the lithium ions that move from the cathode to the anode when the battery is charging.
This chemical reaction is what causes a lithium-ion battery to function. If the chemical reaction is interrupted, the lithium ions react with other components of the battery and cause a thermal runaway. This can happen for many reasons, including battery failure, damage, or end of life.
When a lithium-ion battery fails, it is usually due to one of two things: either the battery is defective, or it has been damaged. In either case, the chemical reaction between the lithium ions and the graphite in the anode is interrupted, and the lithium ions react with other components of the battery.

The Minister of State has outlined a number of challenges facing our urban areas and we would agree that each of the problems highlighted needs to be addressed.
Sinn Féin has been calling for the establishment of a dedicated urban renewal fund for some time now. Sinn Féin is proposing a €250 million urban renewal fund which would be ring-fenced to be used for urban areas. It would be a specific fund, separate from the overall capital budget, to help with the implementation of urban regeneration projects. The allocation of this fund to urban regeneration would ensure that these projects would be given the level of investment they need to be successful. The fund would be used for large projects, such as the regeneration of Ballymun or the development of a new university campus in Dublin. It would also be used to support the small-scale regeneration projects that many communities are undertaking at the moment. This fund would help support the community groups that are coming together to make a difference in their communities. There are many such groups working hard to improve the quality of life in their neighbourhoods. The establishment of this fund would also allow for the prioritisation of urban areas for investment. The fund would target deprived areas that are in need of regeneration and would focus on communities that have been neglected for far too long.

What is Chabad's secret to success? One has to look at the person of the late Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, known to his followers as the Lubavitcher Rebbe. Rabbi Schneerson led his followers to embrace a life of good deeds, selflessness and spiritual growth.
He believed that everyone, no matter what their beliefs, should be treated with kindness and respect. His followers, known as Chabadniks, are a diverse group. They include scholars, rabbis, musicians and artists. They range in age from the very young to the elderly. All of them are united by the Lubavitcher Rebbe's vision of a world filled with kindness, compassion and hope.
The Lubavitcher Rebbe passed away on June 12, 1994, but his legacy lives on. Chabad is in the business of saving lives. It offers guidance and support to Jews who are struggling with their faith, or have nowhere else to turn. Chabad's community centre in Johannesburg, South Africa, for example, provides assistance to hundreds of people who were affected by the recent xenophobic attacks. It has become a refuge for the victims.
Chabad's success is rooted in the words of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who encouraged his followers to work for the benefit of all humanity. The Rebbe was well ahead of his time. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, he was warning about the dangers of global warming.
The Lubavitcher Rebbe had a vision of a world filled with kindness, compassion and hope. The Rebbe's legacy lives on in the work of Chabad centres throughout the world. They are making a real difference in the lives of many people.

species of fur-bearing animals should not be farmed for fur, not only because of the high level of suffering experienced by the animals, but also because of the damage caused to the environment. The Committee was informed that the fur industry uses nearly one third of the world’s mink and one quarter of the world’s foxes, which are all killed for their fur. There are also significant environmental and economic concerns associated with mink farming. Mink are semi-aquatic and the farms have a negative impact on water quality. They also require large areas of land and they often escape and breed with wild mink. This poses a risk to biodiversity. I understand that in Ireland, the European fur industry is worth approximately €250 million, with 85% of the raw fur produced here exported to mainland Europe.
The proposed legislation will mean that the State will no longer allow fur farming. It is welcome that the Government has put forward this Bill. However, the Bill does not go far enough as it fails to prohibit the importation of fur. There is a loophole in the Bill which allows for the importation of fur, and I understand that there is no restriction on the importation of fur from other countries. The Bill also fails to prohibit the sale of fur in Ireland. As a result, the Bill will not achieve its aim of prohibiting fur farming in the State. It will not make fur farming illegal. It will be legal to import fur and it will be legal to sell fur in Ireland. In order to ensure that the Bill is effective it is essential that the Minister provides a clear timeframe for the enactment of the legislation.

We are now aware that the air in schools across the UK is far from healthy. 
A pilot study is to be carried out in Bradford schools.  The pilot will be overseen by the Bradford City Council, and we have been assured that the report will be published.  
The details of the pilot study are as follows:
· 500 air purifiers to be placed in schools across the Bradford area, the number of purifiers in each school will depend on the size of the school.
· The pilot study is to be carried out over a six month period
· The study will be conducted by a health professional and air quality expert. 
The air purifiers being used in the pilot are from a well-known company.
We will keep you updated on the progress of the pilot study, and we are hopeful that the report will be published as soon as it is available.

So, why do separated parents so often struggle to meet the terms of a child maintenance agreement? The main reason is because of the changes to the law in 2014.
Until April 2014, the Child Support Agency (CSA) had the power to compel a non-resident parent (NRP) to pay maintenance under the Child Support Act 1991 and the Child Support Maintenance Regulations 2012, as amended. It had a range of powers at its disposal, including the ability to recover money from an NRP’s earnings and to obtain a court order to make the payments direct to the other parent. If an NRP failed to make payments, he or she would be penalised with an increase in payments and a fine.
The 2014 Child Maintenance Service (CMS)
The CSA was abolished in 2012 and replaced by the CMS. The CMS does not have the same powers of enforcement as the CSA. If a parent does not pay, the CMS can only “name and shame” the NRP by publishing their details online and on social media. If payments are still not made, the CMS can ask the court to make an attachment of earnings order for the arrears. However, it can only make this application after an NRP has failed to pay the maintenance for three months. The court will only make an attachment of earnings order if the parent is receiving a salary. If the parent is self-employed, the court will usually not make the order because the parent’s income is not regular and it would not be practicable to recover the money from the parent’s bank account. This means that, in most cases, the CMS cannot recover any maintenance arrears, whether or not the payment of child maintenance has been agreed by the parents.

duties of employers and employees and the tort of negligence.
As the hon. Member for Enfield North said, the relationship between an employer and employee is a contract of service. Such a contract is a special type of contract. It is a contract of service, which is a contract to serve and to be paid. As such, it is different from the ordinary contract between two people who work together and do not have a contract of service. In an ordinary contract between two people who are not working for a particular company, if they are negligent and someone is injured as a result of their negligence, they are liable in negligence in a civil claim. However, if the injury happens in the workplace, the person who is injured has a right of action against his or her employer, not against the person who caused the injury.
Employers have a duty of care to employees and, more specifically, a duty to provide employees with a safe system of work. The employer is not liable to an employee who is injured because of his or her own fault. However, the employee has the right to sue an employer for breach of the duty of care, which is the duty to provide a safe system of work, and for breach of statutory duty under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.
There is an interesting question about the legal relationship between the employer and the employee and the relationship between an employer and an independent contractor. As I understand it, if the employer is negligent in the way he or she carries out his or her duty of care to the employee and the employee is injured as a result of that breach of the duty of care, the employee can sue the employer, but if the employer is negligent in the way in which he or she carries out his or her duty to the independent contractor and the independent contractor is injured as a result of that breach, the independent contractor cannot sue the employer. He can only sue the person who caused the injury.

Berkhamsted. The ruins of the castle include the Great Hall, the gatehouse and the walls.
The castle was besieged in the 1260s during the Second Barons’ War, with the king’s supporters holding out for 16 days. The castle was also the site of a meeting between King John and the rebel barons in 1216. The castle was finally abandoned during the 17th century, and the castle stones were re-used for other buildings. The Great Hall, though, was saved. This was because it was used as a court for the Assize of Bread and Beer. This was a way of controlling the price of bread and beer, and the court was held there because of the Hall’s large and impressive dimensions.
Today, the castle ruins are looked after by the National Trust. The Great Hall is now an events venue, and can be hired for weddings and conferences. The site is open to the public daily from dawn until dusk.

However, the Court of Appeal made it clear in this case that the right to receive medical treatment is not absolute, and that the law must balance the interests of the child with the interests of the wider community. The Court of Appeal also made it clear that the medical professional is the person best placed to assess whether a particular treatment is in the best interests of the child.
This was not a case about the efficacy of the drug. The Court of Appeal made it clear that there were other drugs which were approved for use in the NHS, which the family also wanted access to, and which were not being prescribed by the consultant.
If a parent wants their child to be given a treatment, there are various things which can be done, which depend on the circumstances of the case. However, as this case illustrates, it is not easy. This case also illustrates that the Court is very reluctant to interfere in a medical decision. In order to persuade the Court to do so, a parent would need to satisfy the Court that the treatment was in the child's best interests, that there was no alternative treatment, and that the medical professional was wrong in his/her assessment of the treatment.
If you are considering trying to get a treatment for your child, it is important that you seek legal advice at the earliest stage to ensure that you are putting your case in the best way possible.

The amendments are technical in nature. It deals with situations where a deposit of less than €40,000 is taken on the signing of a contract, but a deposit of more than €40,000 may be taken on completion of the works. If there is a gap of more than 12 months between signing the contract and completion of the works, the deposit will be returned to the purchaser, less reasonable costs, in full. The amendments will extend this protection to situations where deposits of more than €40,000 are taken on completion of the works, subject to the same conditions. They will also allow for the deduction of reasonable costs, including the cost of obtaining the permission of a local authority and the cost of preparing a completion certificate. Amendments Nos. 19 and 25 are related and will be discussed together.
The amendments will address a significant loophole in the protections provided by section 16. It has been brought to my attention that a property developer could take a deposit of less than €40,000 on the signing of a contract for a major development, but could take a deposit of more than €40,000 on completion of the works. The developer could then defer payment of the deposit for up to 12 months. As the deposit is below €40,000, the protections of section 16 would not apply. The amendments will extend the protections provided by section 16 to this situation and will ensure that the deposit is returned to the purchaser, less reasonable costs, if the developer does not complete the works within 12 months.
The amendments will also allow for the deduction of reasonable costs, including the cost of obtaining the permission of a local authority and the cost of preparing a completion certificate. This is important as the developer may be required to obtain the permission of a local authority and to prepare a completion certificate before returning the deposit to the purchaser.
Overall, the amendments will provide greater protection for purchasers of property and will help to ensure that developers do not abuse the system.

1. They are not the same. A lot of people seem to have this misconception that when someone is not giving enough aid to a country, the country will just fall apart and there will be famine and war. This is not true. Aid can be given to countries in different ways. Some examples are:
a. Military Aid
Military aid is an example of aid that can be very destructive. In fact, military aid has caused wars in the past. For example, a study conducted by the World Bank found that military aid from the United States to Pakistan was responsible for the destabilization of the Pakistani state and the rise of terrorism.
b. Humanitarian Aid
Humanitarian aid is a form of aid that is given to countries that are suffering from a natural disaster or conflict. It can take the form of food, shelter, medicine, or other types of assistance.
c. Developmental Aid
Developmental aid is a form of aid that is given to countries in order to help them develop economically, politically, and socially. It can take the form of loans, grants, technical assistance, and other types of assistance.
d. Economic Aid
Economic aid is a form of aid that is given to countries in order to help them develop economically. It can take the form of loans, grants, technical assistance, and other types of assistance.

The strategy was launched to try to put right what had gone wrong over many years. I am glad to say that maternity services are improving in this country. When we look at the statistics, there are many positive signs of improvement.
I am pleased to say that my constituency of Glasgow North-West is doing better than the average. The figures on the number of midwives in Glasgow North-West are better than the average for the whole of Scotland. We have a better than average number of obstetricians as well. However, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Redcar (Mr. Henderson) said, there are great disparities in the service.
The maternity strategy was launched with great hope. The strategy had some excellent aspirations, such as improving choice, choice of place of birth, choice of consultant, choice of midwife and continuity of care. The strategy was launched to deliver a service in which women could give birth in the place and in the circumstances in which they wanted to do so. However, the implementation of the strategy has been patchy, to say the least. As I said, there are many positive signs in the statistics, but there are also areas of concern.
Women in my constituency are very concerned about the lack of midwives in the area. The statistics are worrying. They show that there has been a decrease in the number of midwives in the past year and a decrease in the number of obstetricians. It is important to remember that the maternity strategy was supposed to have midwives in place of obstetricians. If there are more midwives than obstetricians, it is not a good sign.
The strategy also talks about the number of home births. There is no reason for a woman to give birth at home except that she wants to do so. If there is not a choice, it is a problem. I have been contacted by a number of women in Glasgow North-West about their problems with the maternity strategy.

The Transport Act 2003 provides for the establishment of a public transport regulatory authority and the regulation of public transport services. I am satisfied that the 2003 Act will provide the basis for achieving the objectives of the Bill. The Act confers a number of powers on the authority, such as the power to regulate fares and ticketing, to investigate complaints about standards of service, and to regulate safety and security of public transport services. The authority is also empowered to undertake economic regulation of public transport services, including the power to approve and regulate service contracts between public transport operators and the authority, or any other body or person, and the power to set standards of service for individual transport services.
The public transport regulatory authority will be set up under the Bill and will replace the National Transport Authority, NTA, which was established under the Transport Act 2003. The NTA will be abolished on the enactment of the Bill. The authority will continue to exercise the functions currently exercised by the NTA and it will perform those functions in accordance with the provisions of the Transport Act 2003, as amended by this Bill. It will also perform the new functions conferred on it by the Bill.
The NTA was established in 2003 and its functions were set out in the Transport Act 2003. Its functions include the development and promotion of a co-ordinated public transport system for the greater Dublin area; the promotion of sustainable travel; the development and implementation of a national integrated public transport ticketing system; and the regulation of taxi and private hire services, etc. The NTA's functions will transfer to the authority on the enactment of the Bill.

The Deputy also asked about the national children and young people's well-being monitoring system. This system uses a range of indicators to provide an overall picture of children and young people's well-being. A total of 26 indicators are currently included in the system, including on educational attainment, health, personal well-being and child protection. The system is used to inform policy development and help to measure the impact of policies and programmes. A number of the indicators are used to provide headline indicators for the child poverty strategy, and the indicators are updated annually to reflect current data. The National Children and Young People's Well-being Strategy, which was published in 2019, included a commitment to establish a national well-being monitoring system that would be overseen by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth. The system has been in place for several years and has been very helpful in highlighting important issues related to children's well-being. The system is updated annually, and the most recent update was published in December 2022. The update includes the latest data available on a range of indicators related to children's well-being, including indicators on educational attainment, health, personal well-being and child protection. The update also includes an analysis of the latest data and an overview of trends in children's well-being over time. The update is available on the Department's website. The Deputy has outlined some of the issues he is concerned about in the context of well-being and the child poverty strategy. I would be happy to discuss those issues with him in more detail. I would also be happy to discuss the overall work of the Department, including the well-being framework and the child poverty strategy.

The Bill is a very important Bill. It is about fairness. It is about fairness for fans and fairness for the sports bodies and their members. It is about fairness in terms of pricing and ticketing. It is about making the market more open and more transparent. It is about giving the consumer protection. It is about giving people more power. It is about giving people a greater understanding of how the market operates and how the market works and, most importantly, about giving them a voice and giving them a level of protection that they do not currently have. It is about ensuring that sports clubs, sports bodies and sports organisations can have a fair marketplace in which they can operate. It is about ensuring that they have a voice and that they can make a fair and reasonable profit from the marketplace. It is about ensuring that the consumer is empowered and that he or she can have access to information and that he or she can have protection.
I do not believe that the Bill is perfect. I do not believe that any Bill is perfect. I am sure that after the Bill is enacted, there will be a requirement for changes and for amendments. I am sure there will be a requirement for us to look at it again in the future. However, the Bill is a very good piece of legislation. It is a Bill that is very important to our society. It is a Bill that gives consumers protection. It is a Bill that gives sports bodies the opportunity to have a fair marketplace in which they can operate. It is a Bill that empowers the consumer to have a voice and to protect his or her own rights and interests. It is a Bill that is about fairness for all.

I do not want to be the Member of Parliament for Tottenham who cannot protect its young people from the drug dealers and the gangsters.
It is not right. We have to be able to do something about it. We have to be able to stop those people who are bringing the drugs into Tottenham. We have to be able to find out where the drugs are being stored. We have to be able to get to those people who are selling them. We have to be able to get to those people who are buying them. We have to be able to stop the money that is coming from the drug trade. It is as simple as that. We have to be able to do something about it, and we have to be able to get people off the streets who are involved in that trade. That is the answer.
I have listened to the Minister of State, but that is the only thing that will help my constituents. I have said this before: you cannot have a community in Tottenham that is drug-free and at the same time have an open border with Europe, as the European Union wants, with no controls at all, or with controls that are so weak that they have no deterrent value at all. That cannot happen. It is totally unacceptable. It is not right. It will not happen on my watch.

The most important task for the North is the completion of the Good Friday Agreement and the implementation of the Bill of Rights. The Good Friday Agreement must be implemented in full and all the institutions established by it must be completed and fully functioning. The Bill of Rights will be a vital component of the Agreement and it must be implemented without delay.
There is a real and urgent need to deal with the legacy of the conflict. This includes the completion of the HET, the full implementation of the Patten Report and the appointment of the Historical Enquiries Team.
The Government and the political parties must deal with the issues of policing and justice as part of the political process. We must ensure that the North's policing arrangements are based on the principles of equality, inclusion and protection of human rights. We must also ensure that a modern, accountable and effective criminal justice system is put in place in the North.
We must ensure that the new institutions and political process is accountable and representative. The Assembly must be strengthened by introducing legislation for the creation of a new executive, new legislation must be brought forward to replace the current North-South bodies and the Seanad should have a separate section for Northern representation.
We must also deal with the issue of equality and respect for all. This must include the recognition of Irish as the first language of the people of the North, the development of Irish language and the teaching of Irish.
The economic situation in the North is critical and there is an urgent need for major investment. There must be a comprehensive package of economic measures to address the issues of poverty, job creation and sustainable development.

deal must be in Ireland's national interest. The Taoiseach and I have made it clear to Commissioner Gentiloni that we will be seeking to protect Ireland's national interests. These include maintaining access to the EU's single market, which is worth approximately €5 billion to the Irish economy. We want to ensure that the recovery fund is additional to the MFF and that the Commission's own proposal for the next MFF is respected. It is important that the recovery fund does not crowd out other EU budget headings and that our existing budget allocations are protected, particularly our allocation under the European Social Fund and the European Regional Development Fund. In addition, we want to ensure that the recovery fund is structured in a way that will not distort the economic relationships between Member States and that it will not interfere with our own stimulus package, which we have already deployed.
It is important that the recovery fund and the MFF are closely aligned. This will ensure that the recovery fund is targeted and temporary, and that it will deliver the recovery we all seek. Our approach to the negotiations will be to negotiate in good faith and with an open mind, and to seek to build consensus. We will continue to engage constructively with our European partners as the negotiations on the MFF and the recovery fund proceed.
While the Government is committed to working constructively with our European partners to negotiate an ambitious and effective response to the coronavirus crisis, we also recognise that we cannot spend our way out of the economic difficulties caused by the crisis. We will continue to work with our European partners to ensure that the recovery fund and the next MFF are designed in a way that will bring about a swift, sustainable and green recovery for the European economy.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada is proud to announce today that the Government of Canada is investing more than $2.2 million to support 34 new research and development (R&D) projects across Canada in the manufacturing and agri-food sectors. This investment will create and maintain highly-skilled jobs in Canada, drive productivity improvements and help strengthen our manufacturing and agri-food sectors.
The funding will help companies develop, test and commercialize innovative products and processes that will help them become more productive and competitive.
Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada is providing this funding through the Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP) and the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF).
Today’s announcement builds on our strong record of support for Canadian innovators and businesses across the country. Since 2015, the Government of Canada has invested more than $5 billion to help make Canada a global centre for innovation. Our strategy is helping Canadian companies—in every region of the country—grow and prosper in today’s global economy.
“Canada’s manufacturing and agri-food sectors are vital to our economy and help create jobs for Canadians from coast to coast to coast. The order amends the UK’s official development assistance target, which is set at 0.7% of gross national income. This order amends the target by removing the requirement for the UK to allocate 0.15% of official development assistance to the least developed countries.
The 0.15% target was set in the original legislation. I was surprised to see that it was not included in the initial consultation by the Department for International Development, but it is included in the Government’s response to that consultation. It is worth pointing out that when the target was set in 2015, the Government expected the 0.15% to be met in 2020, but since then the UK’s official development assistance to least developed countries has consistently fallen short of that target.
I am a supporter of the 0.7% target, and I think that it is good that it is enshrined in law, but it is a shame that the UK’s official development assistance to least developed countries has consistently fallen short of the 0.15% target, which is set out in the original legislation. It also proposes that the Parole Board should have the power to grant parole to life sentence prisoners, irrespective of how long they have served. Section 19(8) of the principal Act relates to the circumstances in which the HSE may pay the cost of a medicinal product in advance of reimbursement. It provides that the HSE may pay in advance of reimbursement of the cost of a medicinal product where the HSE considers that there is a substantial likelihood that the medicinal product will be added to the reimbursement list, and where the medicinal product concerned is either an orphan medicinal product or a medicinal product in respect of which a health technology assessment, HTA, is required. Section 3 of the Bill amends section 19(8) of the principal Act by providing that the HSE may also pay in advance of reimbursement the cost of a medicinal product that is not an orphan medicinal product but in respect of which a health technology assessment, HTA, is required and the HSE considers that there is a substantial likelihood that the medicinal product will be added to the reimbursement list. This amendment is intended to align the circumstances in which the HSE may pay the cost of a medicinal product in advance of reimbursement with the circumstances in which the HSE may add the cost of a medicinal product to the reimbursement list. Section 4 amends section 19(9) of the principal Act. Section 19(9) of the principal Act sets out that where the HSE pays the cost of a medicinal product in advance of reimbursement, the HSE shall seek to recover the cost of the medicinal product from the person for whom the medicinal product was prescribed. The Bill amends section 19(9) of the principal Act by providing that where the HSE pays the cost of a medicinal product in advance of reimbursement, the HSE shall seek to recover the cost of the medicinal product from the person for whom the medicinal product was prescribed in the circumstances in which the HSE is entitled to add the cost of a medicinal product to the reimbursement list. Let me make the point more broadly. Devolution is not in any way a temporary matter. It is not a matter of a pause in the exercise of sovereignty, which would allow the Government in Westminster to do whatever it wants for a period of time. Devolution is not like that. It is a permanent settlement, a fundamental and long-term settlement, which is enshrined in the Scotland Act, the Government of Wales Act and the Northern Ireland Act. Those Acts are the foundation of this devolution settlement and they will remain the foundation. Devolution is permanent, and our Bill does not change that.
The devolution settlement is not a temporary interlude in the exercise of sovereignty. It is not a matter of Westminster taking a break from exercising the powers that it had before devolution, and then coming back to those powers after a period. That is not what devolution is. Devolution is permanent, and our Bill does not change that.

We are also enhancing the ability of Elections Canada to enforce the Canada Elections Act. We are establishing a new framework to ensure that political parties are in compliance with election laws and regulations. We are modernizing the enforcement measures to ensure that political parties and candidates are held accountable for non-compliance with election laws and regulations. We are enhancing Elections Canada's powers to conduct audits and investigations. We are clarifying and expanding the authority of Elections Canada to issue orders to political parties, candidates and third parties. We are establishing a framework to enable Elections Canada to use the tools that it needs to effectively enforce the Canada Elections Act.

There have been major changes in society over the past few decades in terms of marriage and family life. There have been increases in the number of marriages and marriages have lasted longer. However, there have also been changes in terms of the number of marriages ending in divorce. Women are now less likely to have children with the man they marry. In 1975, 82 per cent of women with children aged under five years were married to the father of their children compared to 68 per cent in 2013.
It has been estimated that 1,000 children will be born in Ireland this year who will have no relationship with their father. While I welcome the fact that the number of marriages ending in divorce has reduced in recent years, we are still at a stage where one in three marriages end in divorce and more than one in ten marriages end in divorce within five years.

the development of the Kanata sector, and the establishment of a truly unique community spirit. Kanata’s unique story has been documented in a new book published by the local historical society. The book, “Kanata - The Birth of a Community”, written by two of Kanata’s early pioneers, George and Marjorie Hall, was published by the Kanata Historical Society.
The Kanata Historical Society was founded by Bill Teron in 1991, and was originally known as the Kanata Heritage Society. Their mandate is to preserve the history of Kanata for future generations. They have since grown to a membership of over 200 people, and have now published a book documenting the early history of Kanata, including the founding of Kanata Acres, the first major development in the area.
Kanata Acres was originally a 1,700 acre farm owned by the Teron family since 1912. The farm was originally established by Bill’s father, Joseph, and was handed down to Bill and his brother, Robert. The original farmstead was located at the corner of Campeau and Terry Fox, where the Kanata North shopping centre is now located.
Bill Teron’s vision for Kanata Acres was to transform it from a farm into a thriving neighbourhood, with the Teron’s home as the centrepiece of the community. The first home in the development was built by Bill in 1967. Since that time, Kanata Acres has expanded to include the communities of Katimavik, Katimavik-Hazeldean, Kanata Lakes, and Beaverbrook. Today, the Teron’s home is a local heritage site, and is often visited by tourists from all around the world.

We have all been through the most traumatic experience of our lives, and the need for mental health support will be with us for a very long time.
I am pleased to see that, since the pandemic began, £7.5 million has been invested by the Government in 2020 and 2021 to support 18,000 more people to access NHS talking therapies. That is welcome, but it is not enough. I have a couple of suggestions. The first is that we need to create a national network of mental health support for key workers. We have seen that key workers have been stretched to the limit, and the mental health support that they need is not available for them. They cannot take time off work, because they are key workers, and they are unable to get the support that they need. Therefore, we need to create a network of mental health support that is available for key workers.

The United Kingdom is leaving the European Union, and, as a result of that, it will be leaving the European Convention on Human Rights. This is a welcome move, as the European Convention is a piece of socialist legislation, designed by, for and on behalf of the European Union, to be used against us, and it is time that we, as a nation, finally stood on our own two feet and became independent.

The 1998 immigration Act was a disaster. It was one of those rare pieces of legislation that is so bad that everyone agrees it is bad and needs to be changed. But successive governments have avoided doing so, knowing that any change would be unpopular.

So what should be done? I don’t have the answers but I have a few suggestions for starting the discussion.
First, we need a long term, sensible, predictable plan for the numbers that are coming into the country. That will need a sensible plan for the numbers coming out. We need to ensure that we have the resources needed to deliver that policy.
Second, we need to make sure that we have the right skills in the country. To do that we need to have a real plan for the numbers of workers who come in to do low skilled jobs. At the moment, employers can’t be sure that the workers they employ won’t be deported and they are scared to take the risk of employing them. So we get all sorts of problems, including people working illegally and people who are desperate to stay being forced to take low paid, zero hours, precarious work. It was the church that ran the home, and the priest who looked after the interests of the local parish. The state, in the guise of the county council, provided a degree of oversight. The mothers had little choice but to give up their children to the home, and if they did not, they were denied access to a means of living. The home was run by the Bon Secours order. In an interview with the BBC, a former resident of the home recalled the home’s policy of burying the children in the backyard. She claims that she and other residents were asked to bring shovels and fill the backyard with bodies. In the end, the number of infants buried in the septic tank was 796. This number was arrived at after a commission of inquiry. The number was arrived at by digging in the septic tank and counting the bones. These bones included the bones of a full term baby, and the bones of newborn babies. The septic tank, which had been filled with sludge, had been capped off. And yet, it appears that the commission’s findings were not published, and instead, were submitted to the government. The government, in turn, did nothing with the report.
The home has been closed down since 1961.

This legislation is about the creation of a new small companies administrative rescue procedure, a SCAPE. The new process, as I have said, will be for the rescue of small companies that are experiencing financial difficulty and will be voluntary in nature. The new process will be applicable to companies that have up to €3 million in debt and up to 49 employees. The new procedure will be a welcome addition to the existing corporate rescue procedures, examinership and receivership, and will allow for a more flexible restructuring option to be implemented by small businesses.
The new procedure will be administered by an insolvency practitioner, who will be a member of the Society of Chartered Accountants of Ireland, the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Ireland or the Insolvency Practitioners Association of Ireland. The insolvency practitioner will be independent and will not have a financial interest in the company. The insolvency practitioner will need to be approved by the High Court. This is a very important aspect of the legislation. The new process will be an excellent tool for the rescue of small companies. It will allow them to restructure and refinance their debt. It is hoped that this will reduce the need for receivership and liquidation.
This process will enable companies to avoid the necessity of going through liquidation, which would be a very expensive and costly process. It will also reduce the need for insolvency practitioners to go through examinership. This new process will be welcomed by both small companies and the insolvency practitioners who deal with them. It will be a cost-effective and efficient process and will enable small companies to avoid the need to go through liquidation. On the history of the Bill, I am reminded of an episode of "Yes Minister" in which the Cabinet Secretary, Sir Humphrey Appleby, instructs a civil servant to take a piece of paper, write the words "Hansard, 1966", and then, with the greatest degree of solemnity and reverence, lay the piece of paper on the desk. The Bill has a long history that goes back to 1966, when an independent panel was appointed to look into the legal and administrative problems concerning the disposal of the remains of servicemen who died abroad. The panel's report, published in 1967, was wide ranging in its scope and detailed in its recommendations. It was a classic example of how a well-staffed committee with a wide remit can produce a thorough and workable piece of legislation.
I would like to highlight three aspects of the report. First, it was a timely report, because the number of ex-servicemen who had not been recovered was large. It was estimated that in 1965, 5,000 men had not been recovered. Secondly, the report was based on the principle of personal choice. Thirdly, the report was not a matter of principle but a matter of practicality. The report recommended the appointment of an officer-in-charge of the arrangements for the recovery of the remains of the dead and an independent advisory panel to assist the officer in charge.
The report also recommended that the dead should be reinterred or cremated at the choice of the next of kin. It was also recommended that the remains of a soldier who had been killed in action should be brought back to the United Kingdom unless the next of kin chose to have them buried or cremated in the country where the soldier died. This definition does not include a cell, room, or unit that is separated from the general inmate population, a common area, or other designated area only by a wall or partition.
The definition is very broad. It is basically any condition that restricts any of the above areas. For instance, if someone is in isolation for medical reasons, that would be considered administrative segregation under this bill. To help the Government understand how the crisis has affected people, we’ve asked people in the South West about their experiences. You can read the full findings in our Covid-19 in the South West: The impact of the pandemic on people in the South West report.
The report shows that many people have been struggling to afford the basics such as food, energy and rent during the pandemic. More than 1 in 4 people in the South West said they had to borrow money or use credit cards to pay for things during the crisis.
The majority of people who had to borrow money or use credit cards to pay for things during the pandemic are now facing higher energy bills as a result of the cost of living crisis. More than 1 in 4 people in the South West who borrowed money or used credit cards to pay for things during the pandemic are now worried about being able to afford their energy bills.
As the pandemic enters its third year, and the cost of living crisis deepens, we’re calling on the Government to ensure that everyone can access the support they need to make ends meet. This should include increasing the National Living Wage, increasing Universal Credit, and providing the additional £20 per week increase in the Local Housing Allowance.
We also need to see the Government providing more support for people struggling with their energy bills. That should include providing more grants to help people pay off energy debts, as well as improving the Energy Bills Support Scheme so that it covers more people and more of their energy bills.

There are a range of other flood risk management schemes, which are not covered by the Government's flood works capital programme, such as restoration of damaged flood defences. The cost of these works is the responsibility of the owner and/or operator of the flood defence structure. In the case of river flood defences, the Department of Arts, Heritage and the Gaeltacht is responsible for funding works to State-owned structures such as bridges. These are carried out under the national bridges maintenance programme.
The Department of Communications, Energy and Natural Resources and the ESB are responsible for the maintenance of flood defences at ESB dams and reservoirs. The OPW funds the maintenance of flood defences at the 16 major flood relief schemes that are owned by local authorities.
The OPW is also responsible for the maintenance of the 45 major flood relief schemes that were built by it. This is done through an annual maintenance grant to the local authority. The maintenance of flood defence structures is an integral part of the annual capital flood works programme, which is allocated to the OPW by the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform each year. This funding is also used to carry out essential maintenance on existing flood defence structures, where the need is identified through annual inspection and maintenance programmes.
The cost of maintenance of these flood relief schemes is met by the OPW, except in the case of the 16 major flood relief schemes owned by local authorities. In the case of the 16 major flood relief schemes owned by local authorities, the OPW provides funding for maintenance of these schemes on a 50:50 cost share basis with the local authorities.

The Deputy will be aware that the EU’s beef market support schemes are currently being challenged in the World Trade Organisation, WTO, by the US. My Department has been working closely with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, DFAT, and the Attorney General’s Office in relation to this matter. My Department, in conjunction with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, is working with officials in the European Commission on the legal challenge to the EU’s beef market support schemes by the US.
The EU’s beef market support schemes were notified to the WTO in 2019 as a response to a decline in EU beef production. Under the schemes, EU producers receive direct payments for their animals, with an overall budget of €500 million per year, to be distributed through the national authorities in accordance with their respective beef policies.
The beef task force report noted that the EU’s market support measures would continue to be challenged by the US in the WTO. My Department continues to work with the EU in the context of this challenge to ensure the most effective response is made in the interests of Irish beef producers.

The space industry is critical to our national security. Since 2000, the UK space industry has grown at a rate of 8% annually and is now worth £13.7bn and employs more than 42,000 people in the UK. The UK is ranked 2nd in the world in terms of space technology and applications and 3rd in the world for space launch capabilities.
The UK space sector is a major contributor to our economy and will continue to be one of our biggest growth areas.
Earlier this month, we held the first Space Defence Summit, which brought together the UK’s space and defence communities to discuss how we can better integrate space in our defence and security strategies. The summit, hosted by the Defence Space Innovation Network and the UK Space Agency, is a key step in our plans to increase the UK’s role in space and strengthen our ability to use space to protect our security and sovereignty.
The summit also discussed the need to collaborate with allies and partners, which was evident in the announcement of the UK and US Space Data Sharing Agreement. This agreement will improve our ability to exchange space data and information, ensuring a shared vision for the future of our space capabilities.
With increasing tensions around the world, it is crucial that we continue to invest in our space capabilities to ensure the UK can defend its interests and ensure the security of the nation.
