This is the context in which many of Ireland’s workers, including those in hospitality, have come to find employment. The majority of our population – 63% – is female, and as a result, women have contributed to the success of the economy in Ireland in large numbers. They have entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers in recent decades, with women now representing over 50% of the workforce. Over half of all working women are in full-time work.
The hospitality sector is particularly reliant on this female workforce, with almost 75% of the sector’s employees being female. For many of these women, the hospitality sector is the only sector open to them. This is because the sector is an entry point into the workforce for many young people and people from migrant backgrounds. Women in hospitality are more likely to have lower qualifications than those in other sectors, with 47% having completed lower secondary education or less. Hospitality is also the sector with the lowest participation rates in third-level education, with 30% of hospitality employees having completed higher education. Hospitality is also the sector with the lowest share of women in leadership roles. All of this shows the sector’s heavy reliance on a female workforce with lower qualifications and in lower positions.
This is the context for the hospitality sector that we are in right now. And it is one in which we have a responsibility to make sure that workers are treated fairly. At the moment, we are faced with a new reality for hospitality workers in the form of the Covid-19 pandemic. We have seen the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs, and in the case of the hospitality sector, 100,000 jobs have been lost in the last 12 months. These workers are some of the most vulnerable in society, and have borne the brunt of the economic fallout from the pandemic. It is estimated that the hospitality sector will lose 200,000 jobs by the end of this year.

It is not a member of the European Defence Agency, nor has it signed up to the Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) process. Ireland’s policy is that NATO cannot be replaced by a European defence organisation and that an alternative to NATO cannot be pursued at the expense of NATO. In any case, such a project is not feasible given the different perspectives and interests of the EU member states. the manner in which the Minister for Justice and the Attorney General have treated asylum seekers and refugees in the past.
The Irish State has not ratified the UN Convention on Refugees. Instead it has signed the 2003 European Convention on Human Rights. The main difference between the two is that the UN convention obliges the State to take in and to protect refugees, whereas the European convention obliges the State only to consider applications for protection. It does not oblige the State to grant protection.
The result has been the introduction of a series of laws and policies that have been aimed at keeping refugees and asylum seekers out of the country and keeping them in a state of limbo and uncertainty. They are not recognised as refugees and are not allowed to work, or to access welfare or housing. They are housed in direct provision centres, where they are not allowed to bring their families to live with them. They are required to live in these centres for up to seven years before they may be considered for a decision to be made on their application for protection. The decision may be positive or negative. Even if the decision is positive, the process of integration into the State and society may take another ten years or more.
I will now refer to a number of recent cases. I have mentioned the case of the 77 year old Ethiopian refugee, Alem Dechasa, who was detained in a direct provision centre. She was removed from the centre by immigration officers on 20 September 2012. The Minister for Justice and Equality, Mr. Alan Shatter, has failed to explain why she was detained or why she was deported. The Minister has also refused to explain why a court order was issued on 18 September 2012, requiring that she be returned to the direct provision centre, despite the fact that she was already outside the State. Her solicitor, Mr. Gavin Booth, has asked the Minister many questions but has received no answers.

They are a Quebec non-profit organization that promotes active ageing in the Laurentian region and is dedicated to the well-being and happiness of senior citizens.
ANDAL is a leader in active aging and health promotion. Its volunteers have successfully created a number of active aging communities in the Laurentian region, where seniors play a key role in their community. The organization also provides home and community care to seniors. It is a partner in the government's new approach to home care, and its services are provided by the Centre local de services communautaires de Mirabel.

On behalf of the people of Mirabel, I thank ANDAL for its tireless efforts and wish it many more years of success.

In fact, the National Audit Office has predicted that, far from saving the £1.5 billion that the Bill is supposed to save, the NHS will lose £1.3 billion. We therefore want to see the Bill amended.

I am glad to say that the Government are committed to reducing homelessness. We are working hard to deliver on our promise to end rough sleeping for good. We have invested £1.2 billion to tackle all forms of homelessness, and we have doubled funding for the Homelessness Reduction Act 2017. In addition, we have put in place a comprehensive package of measures to tackle rough sleeping. This includes the “Everybody In” strategy, which has a target of getting everyone who is sleeping rough off the streets and into safe accommodation by the end of this month. I am pleased to say that the most recent data show that the number of rough sleepers in England is down by 2% compared with the same time last year.
The hon. Member for Walthamstow (Stella Creasy) mentioned the need for a review of the Homelessness Reduction Act. I am pleased to say that the Government have already committed to this, and we will work with local authorities to deliver this. We are also investing £3.8 billion over the next three years to deliver a range of support to those who are homeless and those at risk of homelessness. I believe that this funding is an excellent start to helping those in need.
I welcome the fact that we are moving forward on many of the things that I am talking about. In fact, we will shortly have the opportunity to have a debate on this issue, which will give us an opportunity to look at the Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 in more detail.

I will begin by looking at the history of the long gun registry. The Liberal government introduced the long gun registry in 1995. It was introduced as a part of Bill C-68, which was an omnibus bill. In 1995, there were many members of Parliament who opposed the gun registry. Some members of Parliament argued that it was unconstitutional. They argued that it would be an encroachment on the rights of the people who wanted to own and use long guns.

As I said earlier, the long gun registry has been controversial since it was introduced. It has faced some very serious challenges in the courts. The fact is, most of the time, soldiers have no idea what they are getting into.
The first day of the battle of Courcelette, which took place near the village of Courcelette, France, on September 15, 1916, was a particularly tragic day for the 49th Battalion. The battalion was ordered to take the German trenches. Before they even arrived on the front lines, the artillery barrage was so thick that the battalion was scattered across the landscape and lost contact with each other. As the soldiers made their way through the barrage, they were blown from their feet by the explosion of a shell.
A few minutes later, the battle was on. The first German trench was taken with the assistance of a tank. The 49th Battalion then ran into two more trenches, but with no tank support, the German soldiers were too strong. The 49th Battalion was forced to withdraw.
By the end of the day, 200 soldiers from the 49th Battalion were dead and 600 were wounded. Some of these wounded soldiers were never able to return to the frontlines, but many more did. In fact, 2,000 of the original 4,000 soldiers were killed or wounded in the first week of the battle of Courcelette.
The 49th Battalion's next assignment was to take the village of Courcelette. The village was captured on September 16, 1916, but the German soldiers were determined to reclaim the territory. They threw wave after wave of attacks against the 49th Battalion, but the battalion held on.
The next day, the 49th Battalion, along with soldiers from the 87th Battalion and the 3rd Canadian Division, attacked the Germans. We know that the Lisbon treaty was not ratified in Ireland because of a narrow majority against it in a referendum. There is a lot of talk about the EU imposing further sanctions on Belarus but the truth is that it has already done so. Moreover, the EU has already taken in some 4,000 Belarusian political asylum seekers.
What else can it do? It can talk, but it cannot attack Belarus for fear of a Russian response.
The most it can do is to continue to impose sanctions on Belarus, hoping that it will find enough Belarusian officials to sanction to hurt the country’s economy and force President Alexander Lukashenko to back down.
The problem is that while Belarus is hurting, so are the many Belarusian companies and individuals who are suffering from the sanctions imposed on their country.

The provision also opens the door for a person who has been subject to a late termination to be able to report the medical practitioner who performed the termination without any risk of legal action by the medical practitioner.
The provision can be contrasted with section 22 of the Health Act 1970 which is designed to protect the confidentiality of a patient. It states that no information regarding a patient shall be disclosed unless the patient gives consent. There are exceptions to this provision, but none of them refer to the disclosure of information that is necessary to protect the health of a third party. The wording of section 22 is deliberately cautious and it is clear that the disclosure of information is prohibited unless the patient gives consent. The disclosure may be made for the purposes of research, teaching, or provision of medical or other services for the benefit of the patient, but it is clear that there is a requirement of patient consent. There is no provision for the reporting of a medical practitioner to the Gardaí. It is therefore difficult to see why the Oireachtas would seek to introduce the reporting provision.
The Irish Medical Council has a Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics which was introduced in 2009 and which requires a medical practitioner to act at all times in accordance with the law and to have regard to the welfare of the patient. It also requires a medical practitioner to behave in a manner which upholds the dignity and worth of every human being. The Code also states that a medical practitioner should act honestly and with integrity. This Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics has been approved by the Minister for Health. It appears that the reporting provision is at odds with the Code and that the reporting provision is therefore not consistent with the law.
It is interesting to compare the reporting provision with the reporting of the provision of abortion services in Northern Ireland.

The committee's role is to facilitate the implementation of the National Recovery Plan and to oversee progress and provide policy direction. The Cabinet committee on economic recovery and investment has been established on a non-statutory basis. The committee reports to the Government and, when required, to the Cabinet.
The role of the committee is to oversee the implementation of the National Recovery Plan, which was approved by Cabinet on 18 May. The National Recovery Plan sets out the Government's response to the economic and financial impacts of the pandemic and is designed to support the economy, support people and support businesses. The plan is made up of a number of actions that will be delivered in the short, medium and long term. The plan was developed in partnership with the social partners and is supported by a high-level steering group that is chaired by the Taoiseach and brings together the key stakeholders involved in its delivery.
The committee's role is to facilitate the implementation of the plan. It meets regularly to oversee progress, provide policy direction where necessary and address issues that arise. The committee has met eight times. The first meeting was held on 8 July. It was chaired by the Tánaiste and Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment, Deputy Varadkar, who also chairs the Cabinet committee on economic recovery and investment. The first meeting was a general update from the relevant Ministers and Departments on the implementation of the plan. The following meetings were chaired by the Ministers of State, Deputies Browne and Humphreys. The committee has been given a very broad brief and oversight of a wide range of issues. Its focus is on the implementation of the plan. The committee has a focus on the short, medium and long-term actions and it seeks to ensure that the plan is delivered in full.

The Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications, Eamon Ryan TD, and the Minister of State with responsibility for the Office of Public Works (OPW), Patrick O’Donovan TD, have jointly announced the allocation of funding for the next phase of the Raised Bog Conservation Programme. This €7.5 million investment will enable the restoration of 2,500 ha of protected raised bogs across the midlands. The programme will be carried out by the OPW’s National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) in partnership with local landowners.
The first phase of the restoration project will be carried out in counties Laois, Offaly, Westmeath, Cavan and Monaghan. The restoration will take place on the bogs of Killarcan, Doonoony, Pollacapple, Currabeg, Annagh, Clooneen, Lough Bane, Togherbeg, Lissaniskey, Lisaniskey, Rathmolyan, Derryfriars, Loughan and Derrygreenagh. The restoration of these bogs will contribute to long-term climate action by removing carbon from the atmosphere and storing it in the bog.
The restoration of peatlands will involve the removal of vegetation and the introduction of wetland wildlife. It will help to improve water quality and reduce the risk of wildfire. In addition, the project will create employment and training opportunities for local communities.
The conservation programme is part of the Government’s commitment to the protection of our natural heritage and will contribute to the achievement of Ireland’s climate action targets. The programme is also in line with the recommendations of the European Court of Justice, which ruled in 2018 that the State had failed to protect its raised bogs under the Habitats Directive.

I am pleased that the Accessible Canada Act, which received first reading on May 31, would establish a framework for a new accessible Canada. This framework will focus on identifying, removing, and preventing barriers to accessibility that are experienced by Canadians with disabilities. These barriers include physical, architectural, communication, information, and technological barriers. This bill would also establish a new accessibility commissioner and a new Canadian accessibility standards development organization.
The first priority of this new commissioner would be to issue a five-year accessibility plan that would identify and set timelines for removing barriers. The commissioner would also be responsible for identifying systemic barriers and developing a plan to remove these barriers.

The good news is that peatland restoration can help us achieve both our climate and biodiversity targets, at relatively little cost. Peatland is the UK’s largest terrestrial carbon store. And if we restore all our degraded peatland, as the government has promised to do by 2030, we would achieve the equivalent of 8% of the carbon emissions cuts needed to meet our net-zero target by 2050.
The bad news is that this is a big ask. In England, we need to restore 180,000 hectares of degraded peatland, or just over 1% of our land area. Peatland restoration is a long-term investment, taking 25-40 years. There is a need for investment now to prepare the ground for this future spending.
We know how to restore peatland. We know where most of the degraded areas are, and we have a good idea of how much it will cost. So, we are calling on the Treasury and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to work out how much money we will need to restore all of our degraded peatland, and commit to spending it now, so that the restoration can start in earnest.
The good news is that peatland restoration can help us achieve both our climate and biodiversity targets, at relatively little cost.
We also need to make sure that money earmarked for peatland restoration is properly spent. This bill, Bill S-204, is a private member's bill introduced by Senator Salma Ataullahjan. It would make it an offence to knowingly receive a financial or other material benefit as a result of the illegal removal of an organ from another person, including for the purpose of transplanting or implanting the organ into the person or another person. The bill would also make it an offence to knowingly possess an organ that has been illegally removed from another person.
The illegal removal of an organ from a person without the consent of that person is a crime under the Criminal Code, but there is no legislation specifically targeting those who participate in the illegal removal of organs or who possess or facilitate the illegal sale of organs.
The bill would apply to a person who commits a prohibited act in relation to an organ, meaning the person would be subject to the same criminal liability as the person who actually removed the organ from another person, even if the person did not actually remove the organ.
This means that if someone is found to have committed a prohibited act in relation to an organ, that person could be charged and convicted of a criminal offence even if he or she did not actually remove the organ from another person. This could include being charged and convicted of a criminal offence for knowingly receiving a financial or other material benefit as a result of the illegal removal of an organ, or knowingly possessing an organ that has been illegally removed from another person.

the airport and aviation sector have been very fortunate in that no major incident has occurred, such as a fatal accident or an aircraft hijacking. As a result of that, the safety of the aviation industry is not questioned to the same extent as it would be in other countries. That means that, as we move forward, we must continue to ensure that the aviation sector is safe and that we are able to protect both the lives of passengers and staff and the economy and livelihoods of the sector and the country as a whole.
The COVID-19 pandemic has also highlighted how the aviation sector can be vulnerable to events that are not related to aviation itself. Indeed, it has proven that if the aviation sector is not able to fly, the economy will grind to a halt. We must therefore look at ways to ensure that our airport and aviation sector can be resilient in the face of future events. In order to do that, we must review the safety and security of the sector. This is what the review by the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice is all about. It is about looking at the structures that are in place, to see whether they are effective or whether they need to be reviewed, modernised or made more flexible. This is why the review is being carried out.
There is no suggestion that the review is being carried out to improve the safety and security of the sector in the face of a terrorist attack. The review is being carried out because of the pandemic. It is about reviewing the safety and security of the sector in the face of events that have nothing to do with terrorism.
This is about the resilience of the sector. It is about ensuring that the sector is safe for passengers, airport workers and airport management in the face of events that could affect the operations of an airport, such as a pandemic, a weather event or a terrorist attack. That is what we are looking at. We are looking at what we need to do to ensure that the sector is safe and resilient.

In the 2019 election, the Liberal government ran on a promise that it would run a surplus in 2021, but that did not happen either. In fact, this year we will have the first deficit under the Liberal government since 2015. The only way that the Liberals can pay for their campaign promises is by adding billions in new debt.

I believe a similar system should be created in the U.S. and it should be given the authority to investigate any marine accident without regard to the flag of the vessel, as is the case with the MAIB. A single person to lead the investigation would provide an accountability structure for the system to work, and it would be one person who would be held responsible for the investigation. The principal investigator would have the authority to direct the course of the investigation and the authority to hire and direct the staff of the unit. It is also essential that the board has the authority to initiate an investigation if a member of the public or a citizen’s group provides evidence of a marine accident. This evidence might come in the form of a ship’s log, photos or witness statements. The board should also have the authority to initiate an investigation if it receives information about a marine accident from an unaffiliated governmental agency, such as the U.S. Coast Guard.
As the investigation proceeds, the board would need to provide the public with information about the investigation as soon as possible. The board would need to set up a web page, and publish information about the investigation in a timely fashion. The board would also need to solicit comments from the public, as well as from marine professionals and experts. A comment form could be posted on the web page, and the board could accept comments by mail or by email.
As an alternative to a board with part-time members, the president of the U.S. could appoint a single person to lead the investigation. The chief investigator would report to the president, and would be accountable to him or her. The president should also appoint a panel of experts to help the chief investigator. The panel should include maritime professionals, marine scientists and marine attorneys.
It is my hope that Congress will take action and enact a maritime accident investigation unit, and that the president will appoint a chief investigator. It is my hope that the president will also appoint a panel of experts to help the chief investigator.

The key point about the offence is that it would be a defence for a company to show that it had reasonable prevention procedures in place. That would mean that it would have to do a risk assessment to find out the risks of tax evasion within its organisation and put in place the right procedures to deal with them. Those procedures would be determined by the company, but they could be things like having whistleblowing policies, which encourage people to raise concerns, having a zero-tolerance approach to tax evasion within the organisation, and making sure that employees and contractors have to sign a tax declaration. They would be risk-based procedures, but it would be up to the company to put them in place and have a defence if it showed that it had done so.

In December last year, my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Transport introduced a new rail package for Britain. That was a bold, ambitious and very welcome package that set out our vision for rail to 2024. It provided a long-term strategic direction that was designed to deliver the best possible railway for passengers and taxpayers alike. It was a package that was based on the principle of value for money, with a clear commitment to a rolling programme of reforms and investment to enhance the value for money of the network.
As we know, the railway is a very complex network. It is one of the most heavily used in the world, with more than 1 billion passenger journeys made each year and 800,000 tonnes of freight transported. The 20,000 employees are doing a great job, and I think that everybody in this Chamber recognises that fact. It is a network that is constantly under pressure, but one that, nevertheless, the Government are committed to improving and modernising.
As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State said in December, there are three key priorities in the rail package. They are to deliver a better passenger experience, to deliver value for money and to deliver a network that is fit for the future. There are many challenges in meeting those objectives, including ensuring that our railways are a good deal for the taxpayer and that value is maximised at every level. The package sets out our plan to deliver that. We will do that by driving up performance and delivery, by making rail more affordable for passengers, by enhancing the rail offering through the franchise system, and by strengthening the commercial and financial discipline of the industry.
The Government are committed to ensuring that the taxpayer gets the best possible value for money. One of the ways in which we can do that is by investing in our rail infrastructure. We are investing more than £37 billion in the rail network between 2009 and 2014, and we will continue to invest,

Alcoa claimed that it had implemented all the measures demanded by the workers but this was denied by the strikers. The new school will serve the communities of Firhouse, Jobstown, Tallaght village, Tallaght, Brittas and Greenhills. It will be a multi-denominational school with a maximum capacity of 500 pupils and will cater for children with special educational needs, including autism spectrum disorder.
The school was identified as a priority in the Dublin South-East Education Taskforce Report and the Dublin South Education and Training Board has submitted a planning application for the proposed school, in line with the terms of the taskforce report and the Tallaght School Provision Plan. The school will also cater for children with special educational needs, including autism spectrum disorder, in line with the recommendation in the report.
The project is funded under the Department of Education’s school building programme and has received planning permission from South Dublin County Council.
The project is being delivered by South Dublin Education and Training Board through the Design and Build Frameworks Office for Government Procurement. The design team is comprised of Limerick-based architects TAKA, Coady Construction and RPS as civil and structural engineers.
The project is due to start on site in early 2023 and is expected to be completed in 2024.

I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the participants and volunteers of the Relay for Life in St. Thomas.

The alcohol industry has a huge influence over government, the media, the law and society in general. For many people, drinking alcohol is a normal, social activity. In other words, it's not just about the individual, it's about us all.
Alcohol is a harmful drug and drinking too much can harm our bodies. Drinking too much alcohol causes around 11,000 deaths every year in the UK and around 1 in 20 people in England are drinking at a level that harms their health.
Alcohol contributes to a wide range of health problems, including liver disease, cancer, depression and anxiety. If we reduce the amount we drink we can reduce the amount of alcohol-related harm in our communities. This is what the alcohol industry should be focusing on.
Alcohol is part of the food industry. Like all food and drink, alcohol should be produced safely, marketed responsibly and taxed so that it's affordable.
The industry needs to look at how it promotes alcohol and how it is advertised, whether it's appropriate for children, and how the tax is set to make sure that alcohol is affordable.
Alcohol is not like other foods – it's a drug and a harmful one. Some drinks are stronger than others, and the more alcohol you drink, the greater the harm.
There are huge differences in the strength of drinks. For example, a single small shot of whisky is 35ml and has an alcohol content of 40%. The same 35ml of wine would have an alcohol content of 10-15%. Even if the 35ml of wine were concentrated into the same strength as the whisky, it would have to be reduced from 250ml to 35ml – that's two thirds less!
The more alcohol you drink, the greater the harm. We drink alcohol in a variety of ways and the more we drink, the greater the harm to our health, relationships and finances.

the fear. Our lives have been turned upside down and the future seems so uncertain. The church has been impacted as well. We are facing the challenges of new ways of gathering for worship. We have been restricted from gathering together in our buildings and many of our beloved ministers, musicians, and pastors have suffered financial loss. We are called to shine the light of Christ in this dark world. There is so much fear in the world and so much fear in the hearts of our people. We are called to live our lives in such a way that we give hope and peace to the world. We are called to love God, to love our neighbors, and to love our enemies. We are called to take up our cross daily and follow the ways of Jesus.
My prayer for us today is that we would allow the light of Christ to shine in our lives. May our lives be filled with the love of Christ and may that love shine in our actions. May our lives be filled with hope in Jesus Christ and may that hope shine in our words and in our prayers. May our lives be filled with the peace of Christ and may that peace shine in our faces and in our actions. May we be the light of the world today!

It is important to note that there is currently no consensus on how to regulate artificial intelligence. Some argue that there should be strict regulations in place, while others argue that there should be minimal regulation. The truth is that it is not yet clear what the best approach is, and the situation is likely to evolve over time.
One of the key arguments in favour of regulating artificial intelligence is the potential for harm. Artificial intelligence can be used to automate a wide range of tasks, from driving cars to diagnosing medical conditions. However, this automation also carries the risk of errors and accidents, which could have serious consequences.
For example, if an artificial intelligence system is used to automate a medical diagnosis, there is a risk that it could make mistakes and give incorrect diagnoses, which could have serious consequences for the patient. Similarly, if an artificial intelligence system is used to automate driving, there is a risk that it could make mistakes and cause accidents.
Another argument in favour of regulating artificial intelligence is the potential for the technology to be used for unethical purposes. For example, artificial intelligence could be used to manipulate people’s emotions, to spread false information, or to engage in other forms of manipulation. Regulating artificial intelligence could help to prevent these types of abuses.
However, it is also important to consider the potential benefits of artificial intelligence. For example, the technology could be used to improve the efficiency of many industries, from transportation to healthcare. What is important is the way in which the Bill sets out a framework for a process in which the House will have a meaningful voice. That is a very important point. The fact that the House is now being asked to have a say on the length of the extension of article 50, rather than simply having to vote on the withdrawal agreement, is a sign of how far we have come in the past few weeks, and is testament to the resolve and the strength of this House in holding to its collective position and ensuring that it has a role in the process of determining the way forward.
The Bill also demonstrates that the House has had a role in determining the extension of article 50, and that the extension of article 50 is now inevitable. We are also seeing a dramatic decrease in the number of local TV stations, with only 11 local TV stations now operating, compared with 21 in 2013, and only six of them are commercially funded. The number of radio stations has remained more or less the same at about 400. When I was growing up, there was only one national radio station—Radio 1. I was surprised to learn that the BBC has 10 radio stations and five national TV channels. That seems a bit excessive.
We have seen the disappearance of local media at a time when we should be increasing them, and we are now seeing the disappearance of local radio. What is the Government’s position on the BBC and its funding? When the BBC licence fee was last debated, the Minister said that it was vital to keep it, because the BBC is a great British institution and is the envy of the world. However, we are seeing cuts in local radio stations and in the BBC’s local radio coverage.
We have a situation in which the BBC has its licence fee guaranteed and paid for by all of us, and yet local radio stations are losing money, and it seems that they are being sold to the highest bidder to make a quick buck. I ask the Minister, is he content to see local radio stations in danger, and will he commit to making sure that BBC local radio stations are properly funded? If the BBC cannot pay for that, and it is not going to be included in the licence fee, will he commit to increasing the licence fee to pay for it? We cannot have a situation in which local radio stations are struggling and being lost while the BBC has a guaranteed licence fee and is allowed to expand its online operations. I look forward to the Minister’s response.

There is no silver bullet to ending this pandemic, but one thing we know for sure is that the vaccine is the best way out. However, the vaccine rollout is not moving as quickly as it should and people are understandably frustrated.
We need more vaccines, but we also need to know that the doses that we do have are getting into arms as quickly as possible. We need to be focusing on expanding distribution sites, not expanding the list of places people can book. This is why I am calling on the government to stop playing politics with the vaccine rollout and to focus on delivering results.
While the Prime Minister has the power to change the eligibility rules, I am not convinced that it would lead to any significant increase in the number of people that are vaccinated. The reason for that is that, right now, the number of people who have been vaccinated in Canada is not the issue, it is the supply of vaccines. The problem is that Canada is not getting a fair share of the vaccines that we have paid for.
While the Prime Minister likes to brag about the billions of dollars we have given to the pharma companies, he is failing to mention that he is not actually getting us the vaccines we paid for. The government is failing to deliver on the commitments that it has made to Canadians and we need the Prime Minister to start taking the vaccine rollout seriously.
We also need to consider the importance of procuring and distributing vaccines in the road to rebuilding our economy and helping Canadians get back to work. There is no recovery without widespread vaccination. This brings me to a question that I hear from constituents every day: When will they be able to get the COVID-19 vaccine?
There is no silver bullet to ending this pandemic, but one thing we know for sure is that the vaccine is the best way out. However, the vaccine rollout is not moving as quickly as it should and people are understandably frustrated.

The fight for women’s suffrage didn’t end in 1918, and there are still battles to be fought for women’s rights. But it’s crucial we remember the sacrifices of the women who came before us.
I’m not one of those who believe that we should be celebrating the 100th anniversary of a law that gave some women the right to vote, while we’re still fighting for equal pay and fighting against domestic abuse. But we must remember that this 100th anniversary is a step forward.
As the British Prime Minister, Theresa May, said, this is “a day to celebrate the tireless work of the suffragists and suffragettes, to celebrate the courage of those who fought for the vote and to celebrate the first women who were elected to Parliament.” So let’s celebrate. We must also consider the impact of shark finning. Many of you will have heard of this practice, whereby shark fins are cut off and the bodies are dumped back into the sea, leaving them to drown. The fins are then sold on to make soup, a delicacy in many countries, with China being the largest consumer. The demand for shark fin soup has become so excessive that shark populations are being decimated, with some species declining by up to 99%. Shark populations are in decline because of the way that they are fished. Some shark species take a long time to reach sexual maturity and have a relatively low number of young. Other species are targeted because they are thought to be dangerous to humans and are killed as a result of mistaken identity.
The UK must take responsibility for its own actions and support a complete ban on shark finning in UK waters. We must also take action to protect the shark populations in our seas. I urge the UK Government to follow the example of the EU and ensure that the UK has robust legislation in place to protect sharks and that we work with other countries to protect shark populations globally.
The UK should also take a more active role in protecting sharks and in developing solutions to the problem of overfishing, as it is one of the largest contributors to the problem. In 2008, the UK Government was asked to consider signing the UN Agreement on the Conservation of Sharks, a legally binding agreement that commits all parties to protecting sharks and taking measures to conserve them. Unfortunately, the Government decided not to sign the agreement because of the economic implications. I have been told that it was because the shark fin trade was worth £2.5 million to the UK economy, which is an argument for continuing to support this barbaric practice, not for ending it. I join the hon. Member for Glasgow Central in paying tribute to the late John Smith. I served alongside him in the Labour party and as a Member of Parliament. He was a man who was much loved and admired, and who left a big hole that has never been filled. I was particularly saddened that he did not have the chance to become Prime Minister, because he would have been a great one. He had many strengths, but the most important was his humanity. He was always prepared to listen to the arguments of those around him and to take account of those arguments. He was also prepared to change his mind, and that is a rare quality in politics. He was an inclusive politician, who looked to the future and was not obsessed with the past. He was a great moderniser, and he was able to bring into the Labour party people who had never been there before. He was an internationalist, who saw the world not through the prism of whether it was “with us” or “against us”, but through a much more nuanced approach. He was the first Labour leader to call for the reunification of Ireland. He was a great politician, and we have lost a great servant of our nation.
I also pay tribute to my right hon. Friend the Member for Doncaster North (Edward Miliband), and I join the hon. Member for Glasgow Central in thanking him for his outstanding contribution to the debate, which was conducted with grace and courtesy. He is a man of considerable intellect, but he is also a man of great humanity. He has worked tirelessly to try to bring the country together. I wish him well in whatever he does in the future. I know that he will continue to be an outstanding public servant.

This is encouraging news and further emphasises the importance of our indigenous industry in contributing to our seafood sector and our national balance of payments.
As the Minister is aware, there are serious challenges facing the industry, particularly in relation to cost competitiveness and market access. However, with our clean waters and world class seafood, there is huge potential for the aquaculture industry. I am hopeful that we can grow the industry to help secure a sustainable and long-term future for the sector.
The Government’s action plan for the implementation of the new National Strategy for Aquaculture Development 2014-2020 is being progressed. The plan is aimed at ensuring that the potential of the Irish aquaculture sector is realised to the benefit of the local communities, national economy and the wider sector. It is also aimed at maximising the economic, social and environmental potential of aquaculture as a key sector of the blue economy.
This strategy is a key part of the Government’s seafood development programme which aims to enhance the contribution of the seafood sector to Ireland’s economic growth. The programme, which was published in March 2017, sets out the measures required to deliver the Government’s vision of the seafood sector contributing €1.25 billion to the Irish economy by 2025.
I am pleased that a new €2 million aquaculture fund has been announced to support the industry. This fund will provide €500,000 per annum for three years for new market and product development. This

That is why I was pleased when the Prime Minister announced that the Government would be consulting on how best to ensure that all patients, regardless of their circumstances, receive the mental health treatment they need. However, the consultation document was disappointing and failed to address many of the concerns raised by organisations such as the Royal College of Psychiatrists. The Government have acknowledged that there is an unmet need for mental health services, but the document appears to be more of a PR exercise than a genuine attempt to tackle the problem.

“by 2020, to improve access to specialist mental health care for patients with the most complex needs and by 2023/24 to reduce waiting times for specialist mental health treatment from 72 to 28 days for the majority of patients.”

She then went on to speak about the need for reconciliation and how the Christmas story brought “hope of peace with justice” to the world.

This theme was then taken up by the Archbishop of Canterbury in his 2018 Christmas Day sermon, which referred to the importance of “building relationships between different people and different communities”. The reality is that Covid has revealed the poor state of the HSE and the huge task of trying to improve it.
Covid has shown that the HSE is in need of an enormous amount of investment and change. We must learn from the mistakes of the past to rebuild the HSE into a modern, fit-for-purpose, world-class health system.
That is why we are calling for a massive injection of capital investment of €3.5 billion into the HSE. The HSE has been consistently underfunded over the past decade and we believe that a €3.5 billion annual investment is necessary to bring it up to the level required. This is necessary to build much needed capacity across the health service, including additional hospitals, health centres and primary care.
That is also why we believe that the HSE must be reformed and that we must put in place a new model of health services. We want to see a public health system that is patient-centred and accessible for all, with an emphasis on prevention and early intervention. We want to see a system that is responsive to the needs of the people it serves, and that is transparent and accountable.
We want to see a system that is built on the principles of solidarity, and that ensures that no one is left behind. We believe that everyone in Ireland should have access to world-class healthcare, regardless of their income or background.
We will make a major investment in the HSE to bring it up to the level of a world-class healthcare system.
We will reform the HSE to put in place a new model of health services that is patient-centred and accessible for all.
We will put in place an independent Covid service within the HSE to ensure that we have one of the most comprehensive testing and tracing systems in the world.

The Department for Work and Pensions was created in 2001 and was the first Department to be launched under the Labour Government. It was a merger of two previously existing Departments—the Department of Social Security and the Employment Department—which had both been created in 1989. The intention behind the merger was to create a Department that would be more responsive to people’s needs. I think that it has achieved that, although the two Departments that existed previously were very different. The Department of Social Security, as the name suggests, focused on benefits, whereas the Employment Department was focused on the active labour market and employment policy. The Department for Work and Pensions has a far broader remit, and I think that that is to its credit.
The two Departments that preceded it—the DSS and the Employment Department—had a joint aim. They both wanted to support people to be in work and to be independent. We are determined to ensure that the North's people are not consigned to a never-ending cycle of instability and crisis. We are committed to achieving a fresh start for everyone on this island, irrespective of identity, tradition or religion. The new Government will be open to dialogue with all the parties on the North of Ireland.
We have a clear mandate from the people to deliver stability and prosperity. We are determined to make a decisive break with the instability and uncertainty of the past. We will ensure that the Government is not subject to the whims of any other party. We will deliver real change, starting with a new political system based on equality and integrity.
In the forthcoming months, the Government will move quickly to secure the passage of the Dáil (Assembly) Constituencies (Northern Ireland) Bill through the Oireachtas. This is an essential precondition to the Northern Ireland Assembly becoming operational. We also intend to bring forward legislation to reform the Irish language and Northern Ireland's cultural institutions, to modernise the 1920 Government of Ireland Act and to deal with the legacy of the past. These Bills will be passed this year.
We will ensure that the Border Poll promised in the Programme for Government is held within the lifetime of the next Government. We will also work with the British Government to ensure the full implementation of the Good Friday Agreement and the full and final implementation of the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland.
The North of Ireland faces many challenges. It has suffered from a lack of investment and the absence of strategic development. It has been characterised by low wages, poor public services, high unemployment and emigration. It is essential that the North's economy is strengthened and its people are empowered to determine their own future. We will work to create opportunities for businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises. We will work with the British Government to establish a Northern Ireland Investment Bank.

As part of that strategy, the Government has committed to the establishment of a State Land Development Agency which will be focused on maximising the development potential of State lands.
The LDA is a new body established in July 2019 and its primary objective is to ensure that the development potential of State lands is realised in a manner that is consistent with the national planning framework, the national development plan and other relevant national policy and strategy. The LDA is responsible for managing the development of State lands, in particular State lands that are designated as strategic housing land. The LDA is also responsible for the promotion of the development of State lands for the purposes of providing affordable housing. The LDA is also responsible for the management of the State land bank and the State's housing stock.
As I have outlined, the LDA was established in 2019. The agency has a number of significant initiatives under way. These include the strategic housing development process for the promotion of strategic housing development sites, the development of a land release strategy, the development of an affordable housing strategy and the delivery of an affordable housing programme. The LDA has also been working on a number of projects for the delivery of affordable housing. These include the provision of affordable housing in communities in need and the provision of affordable housing in urban regeneration areas.
The Government has been keen to ensure that the LDA is independent in its role and is free to operate without interference from other State agencies. To that end, the Government has ensured that the LDA has a Board of Directors that is independent of the State. As I was leaving, a gentleman came into the hall and asked me to deal with an issue he was having with his bank. I advised him to contact my office and I would follow up on the matter. There is a problem with how the banks are dealing with this matter. I contacted the Irish Banking Federation in respect of this and I am awaiting a response. I understand that the Government has also been in contact with the banks about this matter. The banks must understand that the Government is giving employers the option of using the temporary wage subsidy scheme as a stop-gap until they can get their businesses back on track.
I would not be surprised to find out that the banks are refusing to deal with this matter because they want to stop the temporary wage subsidy scheme from being used, but the reality is that there are many people who have been impacted by the Covid-19 crisis. They need the option of availing of this scheme in order to get back on their feet. We need to make sure that it is up and running as soon as possible. I understand that it is up and running from the end of May, but many people will need to get back to work immediately.
The banks have to understand that the Government has taken over the responsibility of paying wages. People need the option of being able to go back to work immediately and, in order to do that, they need to be able to avail of the temporary wage subsidy scheme. I ask the Minister to look into this issue and ensure that the banks are not refusing to deal with the temporary wage subsidy scheme.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to this very important bill, which is in response to a report from the Standing Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology titled “Euthanasia and Assisted Suicide: The Case for Caution”.
I would like to start by congratulating Senator Pamela Wallin for her incredible work chairing that committee and leading the way on this very important issue.
I would also like to thank the members of the committee for their efforts in conducting such a thorough review of this issue. In the end, I am not sure that the bill itself is the perfect solution, but I do believe that the committee report is a solid piece of work that makes a number of recommendations that I would agree with and that I hope the government will act on.
The main point that I would like to make is that, with this bill, we are dealing with a very complicated and sensitive issue. There are so many aspects to consider, and all Canadians will have their own opinions on what the government should or should not do.
While we are debating this bill, I think it is important to remember that we are not debating any specific medical cases or whether or not someone in particular should be able to access assisted suicide or euthanasia. This bill is not the place for those discussions. The bill is a proposal for a law that would allow the federal government to regulate assisted suicide and euthanasia.

Following a detailed review of the costs of legal advice, we have agreed that this should be funded by the Scheme Administrator at a fixed rate of £250 per postmaster.

Postmasters will need to apply for this initial legal advice, and we will process applications from a list of legal advisors which has been provided to us by the Association of British Postmasters’ Scheme (ABPS).  This list has been provided to us as the best available information for postmasters who are seeking legal advice on their claim.
The list includes firms which have already agreed to represent postmasters under a contingency fee arrangement.
We have also provided details of this list to the postmasters’ lawyers who have been engaged by the ABPS and the Post Office.

In any event, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-11, An Act to amend the Criminal Code (investigation of missing persons), today. This is a bill that is very important to me, and I am thankful for the opportunity to talk about it.
The legislation would allow police and prosecutors to bring charges against individuals who do not report a missing person to police within a reasonable period of time. At the moment, there is no such requirement, so people can simply wait. Sometimes the person is found, and all is well, but sometimes the person is not found and a crime is committed. We have a lot of information on how many people are missing in Canada, but the number of missing people is unknown because there is no requirement for individuals to report someone missing to police. Sometimes people are not reported missing for many months, and sometimes they are not reported missing at all.
This is a very serious matter, not just for families but also for law enforcement officers who are trying to do their jobs.
The bill is very simple. It is about two pages long. The current legislation gives a police officer the authority to demand information from an individual, but this bill would make it mandatory for people to report someone missing to police. The onus is on the individual to provide the information. It would be the individual's responsibility, and I think that is the right thing to do.
This is a very serious matter, not just for families but also for law enforcement officers who are trying to do their jobs. They have no idea who the missing persons are, and therefore cannot investigate the crime. That means that a lot of missing persons will never be found. This bill will allow police to get the information they need to do their jobs.
I will not take up too much time on this bill. It is pretty straightforward. If someone knows where someone is, they are obliged to report the information to police

Although the Bill is relatively straightforward, its provisions are important, and I am grateful for the commitment to the Bill from the Government and the other place. I also pay tribute to the House of Lords for its work in scrutinising the Bill and passing it with such alacrity and with only one amendment, which we have accepted and included in the Bill. The Bill’s provisions are straightforward, but they are important and will make a difference to the lives of thousands of people.
The Bill will make the law clear in three main areas. First, it makes clear the law relating to the protection of personal data by the police and other law enforcement agencies, and it will provide a new legal basis for the processing of personal data for the purposes of preventing, detecting or investigating a serious crime. Secondly, the Bill updates the law relating to the police’s ability to retain certain categories of information. Thirdly, the Bill will extend the power of law enforcement to access the communications data of those who pose a risk to the public, but only with the approval of a judicial commissioner. The Bill will make a positive difference to the lives of thousands of people and improve law enforcement’s ability to protect the public from harm.
The new legal basis for the processing of personal data for the prevention, detection and investigation of serious crime will enable police and other law enforcement agencies to process personal data that is necessary for these purposes, subject to certain safeguards. The law must be clear that personal data is used only where necessary and proportionate, but the safeguards built into the Bill will ensure that it is used only where necessary and proportionate. The safeguards include a requirement that the processing of personal data must be necessary for the prevention, detection and investigation of a serious crime, and a requirement that the personal data processed must be of sufficient relevance to the crime in question. The Bill will also require law enforcement agencies to take certain steps to minimise the intrusion on the privacy of individuals whose personal data is processed.

What are smart motorways?
Smart motorways are designed to reduce congestion and make better use of the existing roads. These roads are fitted with variable speed limit signs, so that the speed limit can be adjusted depending on traffic and weather conditions. The lanes on smart motorways are also electronically controlled, so that a lane can be closed if necessary. This allows the flow of traffic to be managed more effectively, reducing congestion.
The introduction of smart motorways has been controversial, as there have been concerns about safety. In particular, there have been concerns about the use of the hard shoulder as a live traffic lane, as this can lead to accidents if drivers are not aware that the lane is open to traffic. There have also been concerns about the lack of refuge areas on some smart motorways, as these can make it more difficult for drivers to exit their vehicles in an emergency.
What to do if you’ve been involved in a motorway accident
If you’ve been involved in a motorway accident, then it’s important to seek medical attention as soon as possible. You should also contact the police to report the accident, and you may also need to contact your insurance company. If you’ve been injured in the accident, then you may be eligible to make a claim for compensation. Your personal injury lawyer will be able to advise you on your options and will take your case forward on a No Win, No Fee basis.

The 2030 target and the first two carbon budgets will need to be consistent. If the Advisory Council sets the first two budgets to achieve the target and the government subsequently amends the target, the government will have to reconsider the budgets.
Section 6A(5) of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 introduces a new target for 2030 of at least 63% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared to 2018 levels. The target is binding on the government, in the sense that it must be complied with.
The new target is binding on the Advisory Council to the extent that it must take it into account when setting the first two carbon budgets. The first two carbon budgets will be set by 15 September 2023. In setting the first two carbon budgets, the Advisory Council will be required to consider “all relevant policies, measures, targets and plans”, including the new 2030 target.
There is uncertainty as to the extent to which the 2030 target is binding on the government. Although it is binding on the Advisory Council, the Advisory Council is not a decision-making body. It is the government that must set the budgets by 15 September 2023. The Advisory Council must recommend budgets to the government. However, the government will have the power to amend the budgets. Therefore, it is arguable that the 2030 target is binding indirectly on the Advisory Council

Let us be clear: the Secretary of State’s refusal to act is a breach of the ministerial code. The Stigma Project is launching a global campaign on social media to change the conversation.
To change the conversation about drug use, we need to be thoughtful and intentional about the language we use. Changing the language we use to describe people who use drugs is one of the most important ways to shift the narrative and challenge stigma. This is an important way to address the issue of stigma. The UNODC Stigma Project can help by providing alternatives to the language we use to describe people who use drugs.
The Stigma Project is launching a campaign to change the conversation about drug use by using social media. This is a great opportunity to join the conversation and spread the message that people who use drugs are not bad, they are people with needs and desires just like everyone else. I want to begin by providing a little background. On April 1, 2020, the House of Commons resumed sittings following its suspension due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the need for public health measures, the House adopted a hybrid format for sittings. In this hybrid format, members could participate in sittings from both inside and outside the chamber. This was a significant departure from the usual practice, as members had always been required to be physically present in the chamber in order to participate.
The hybrid format allowed the House to resume its normal business while respecting the need to mitigate the spread of COVID-19. It allowed us to continue to do the work that we were elected to do, while following public health advice.
Unfortunately, the hybrid format did not last. On December 16, 2020, the government made an unprecedented move and adopted new rules, without any consultation with the House, which effectively ended the hybrid format. This was done in order to allow the government to ram through legislation, without the proper parliamentary scrutiny and debate that the public expects and deserves.
The new rules require that members be physically present in the chamber in order to participate in sittings. This means that members who live in other provinces, who may be in isolation, who may have health conditions or who may have other personal or professional obligations that prevent them from travelling to Ottawa on short notice, are unable to participate in sittings.

I am delighted that the report has concluded that Select Committees should have a power to summon a person to appear before them. I have long held the view that this would be a useful development. We are very grateful to the previous Backbench Business Committee for recognising the potential value of such a power and granting time for this inquiry. The report is a clear indication of how much the Backbench Business Committee is interested in the House’s procedures.
I am also grateful to the Committee for its recognition of the power of the Chair of the House to deal with the more serious breaches of privilege, such as the contempt of the House, by the members of a Committee.
In the Committee’s view, it is not necessary to enact legislation to confer the new power on Select Committees, but I would emphasise that the Committee’s recommendation is entirely consistent with the constitutional principle that the exercise of parliamentary privilege remains within the exclusive authority of the House. The Committee’s recommendation is consistent with the principle that the Chair of the House is the ultimate guardian of privilege and that the Chair of the House has the power to deal with any serious breach of privilege, including a contempt of the House.

Billy was a key player in the team that won the League in 1966, the club's third in a row, and then the European Cup in 1967. However, in June of that year, Stein gave him the opportunity to play for Scotland, a chance he grasped with both hands and one which resulted in a stellar international career spanning more than 20 years. During that time, Billy was a member of the Scotland team that won the British Home Championship in 1967, 1968, 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, 1978, 1979, 1980, 1981 and 1982. He was part of the team that finished second in the FIFA World Cup in 1974 and third in the UEFA European Championships in 1976. His 79 international caps also included five for the Scottish League in 1973 and 1974.
Following Jock's untimely death in September 1985, Billy was appointed caretaker manager at Celtic Park, leading the team to a 3-0 win over Motherwell in his first game in charge. He was given the job on a permanent basis in December 1985 and he led the team to a 6-2 win over Dundee in his first game in charge at the end of the month.
After a shaky start to his first season as manager, Billy steered Celtic to a famous League and Cup double in 1986/87. That season marked the start of a decade in which Celtic lifted the League championship seven times and the Scottish Cup on four occasions.

The UK is one of the few economies in the world, if not the only one, that can function efficiently in three currencies. The pound, the euro and the US dollar. That, in itself, is a great advantage.

This will help to keep our economy buoyant.
We have great natural resources, which we can exploit in the right way, using the latest technology. The UK is a leader in this field, and we will be able to develop our strengths. We have a very good education system, and this will help to train up the next generation of talent.

member's bill, the Office of the Commissioner for Responsible Business Conduct Abroad Act.
It is no secret that Canadians are concerned about the behaviour of Canadian companies abroad. I am concerned about the behaviour of Canadian companies abroad.
My bill would create an independent office of the commissioner for responsible business conduct abroad, reporting directly to Parliament, to investigate allegations of misdeeds by Canadian companies and report on the findings.
This would increase public awareness of the importance of responsible business conduct, it would put pressure on companies to act responsibly, and it would increase the chances that companies would be held accountable when they do not.
A recent poll found that 90% of Canadians believe it is important that Canadian companies operating abroad adhere to Canadian values and standards of behaviour.
The proposed commissioner would conduct investigations, produce annual reports to Parliament, and provide reports to the public, upon request.

The current Canada Post labour dispute is no different. It is a dispute between the employer and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, and it is about collective bargaining. It is not, as some have suggested, about the postal service itself. In fact, Canada Post and CUPW have been able to negotiate new agreements with the vast majority of union members and the vast majority of Canada Post employees have continued to work.
Canada Post has offered CUPW the same 3% wage increase for each of the next three years. That is more than the average wage increase for all Canadian workers in 2014. Canada Post also proposed an additional $700 million over the next three years to increase the service standard for regular letter mail, to 10 days or less, up from its current 11-day standard. This would provide for a two-day improvement in the service standard. This is a significant investment.
Canada Post has also offered CUPW a new contract that would create more than 7,500 new jobs. We can agree that these are very good offers that address the issues that are important to Canadians.
However, CUPW has refused these offers and has continued to strike. I understand that the Canadian Union of Postal Workers is a member of the Canadian Labour Congress, the CLC. The CLC, of course, is a signatory to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The CLC is a proud supporter of this important Canadian charter, and I am proud to say that our government is, too. The charter protects and promotes fundamental freedoms and democratic rights, and it includes a guarantee of the right to peaceful assembly. That is the right to peaceful assembly.
Now, Canada Post is not a union. It is a crown corporation, a vital piece of infrastructure that the Government of Canada is responsible for. A strike by a crown corporation is a strike against the Government of Canada.

As you know, we have three levels of government. The federal level, the provincial level and the municipal level. When you vote for the municipal level, in most places, you are actually voting on a list.
In the last municipal elections in Montreal, I was a candidate. And you voted on a list. You voted for a party list. So, if you wanted to vote for the city council, you had to vote for a party list. You voted for the Green Party list, or the Liberal Party list, or the CAQ list, or the Québec Solidaire list. This is the system that’s used in Montreal, as well as in a number of other jurisdictions across the country.
But the problem with this system is that it’s not really a direct system. You don’t vote for individual people, you vote for lists. Now, the reason that this has been done, historically, is that it has been done to encourage a better turnout. If you’re voting for a list, then it’s easier for you to understand the mechanics of voting and to participate in the process.
But here’s the problem. When you’re voting for a list, you are actually voting for a group. You’re not voting for an individual. You’re not voting for somebody that you know and who represents you. So, when you do vote for a list, you’re voting for a group. And, unfortunately, the system is set up in a way that the people who actually get elected to these positions are not the people who you actually elected.

I have been asked a lot about the dangers of cannabis. It is dangerous, like any substance that is not used appropriately. However, when we are talking about how to legalize and regulate cannabis, we have to look at the dangers of alcohol and tobacco. They kill far more Canadians than cannabis.
I think it is important to realize that cannabis legalization will allow us to go after organized crime, undercut their profits, and create a legal market where people can use cannabis responsibly, just like alcohol. That is important. We will never be able to legalize cannabis 100% and get rid of organized crime. It is not going to happen, but we can get rid of the profits. That is what we need to do.
The legalization of cannabis is also important to Indigenous people and their communities. I am the member of Parliament for a large riding in northern Alberta. It is a big area and it includes 10 different First Nations communities.
My riding is home to a lot of Indigenous people. They have to use cannabis. However, they cannot use it legally. They have to buy it from the black market, and they are being undercut by organized crime. They are not able to use it legally.
I think that is important for us to understand. We have to recognize that legalization of cannabis will help a lot of people who are marginalized, who are living in poverty, and who are living in communities where there are no jobs and no opportunities. Legalization of cannabis can help a lot of those people.
I have also been asked a lot about driving while impaired. I believe in the legalization of cannabis. However, I do not believe in impaired driving. When I was a police officer, I arrested a lot of people for impaired driving. It is a serious crime. It kills people. It kills innocent people.

The Government made a commitment in their White Paper that
“fundamental rights…will continue to be guaranteed in the UK.”
The Government did not say that fundamental rights would be guaranteed in the same way, but that is what we need. The White Paper has no details as to how this will be achieved, and it is now three and a half months since the publication of the White Paper, with no sign of a UK Bill of Rights or a statement as to how the Government will deliver on their White Paper promise. Meanwhile, we have seen the publication of the first draft of the European Union (Withdrawal) Bill. The draft Bill, which is now subject to consultation, has many good points, but it does not guarantee fundamental rights in the way that the Government have promised. In fact, it goes against the Government’s promise.
There are four ways in which the draft Bill fails to guarantee the protection of fundamental rights. The first is that it excludes the EU charter of fundamental rights from retained EU law. The second is that it gives Ministers powers to disapply retained EU law. The third is that it provides no definition of the scope of retained EU law. The fourth is that it omits the “principle of non-retroactivity” from retained EU law, which means that, after Brexit, the Government could repeal any law that was passed in the UK after the date of the withdrawal of the UK from the EU, even if that law had previously been approved by the European Parliament or the Council of the EU. That is a massive risk for UK citizens.
The draft Bill is silent on what the scope of retained EU law is. The Government need to define clearly the scope of retained EU law. They must not be vague. At

cost of autism related therapies and supports per child per year is between €13,000 and €21,000, depending on the individual’s needs.
Parents are being forced to work more hours just to make ends meet. But this leaves little time for the essential care and support needed for their children with autism. It also means that they are not present in the home when the school bus arrives. A recent survey by Enable Ireland found that 80% of families surveyed had to miss work to accompany their child on the school bus, due to a lack of special needs assistants.
The majority of these families live below the poverty line. More than 50% of families who responded to the survey by Enable Ireland have an income of less than €20,000, and 40% have an income of less than €15,000. 84% of families have less than €1,000 left over after paying for their child’s therapy and special needs support.
The financial and time pressures of raising a child with autism can be overwhelming. Parents are constantly weighing up what is best for their child against what is affordable. Many families have had to make the heartbreaking decision to stop therapy for their children because they simply can’t afford it. It is a reality that no family should ever have to face.

The Act does not apply where a business is going into liquidation or where the employer is acting on behalf of the Insolvency Service. This is because the duties imposed by the legislation would be likely to interfere with the normal functions of a liquidator in winding up a company.
The Act does not apply to employees whose employment has already ended. For example, where the employer has notified employees of their redundancies and the redundancy has already taken place before the 30-day period expires, there will be no obligation on the employer to inform and consult. However, an employer will be obliged to consult where the redundancy does not take effect until after the expiry of the 30-day period. In that situation, the employer will be obliged to consult even though the employee has been notified of the redundancy and a contract of employment has terminated.
The obligation to inform and consult does not apply where the employer is proposing to make individual redundancies unless the redundancy is part of a larger redundancy exercise which involves more than 20 employees and a collective redundancy.
The Act does not apply where a redundancy is a result of a change of circumstances beyond the employer's control. For example, where an employer closes an undertaking due to severe economic or market conditions, there would be no obligation to inform and consult.
There is no statutory definition of 'undertaking'. However, it has been held that 'undertaking' is not confined to the establishment of the employer but includes all the various branches of the same business, including all the various sites, works or workshops of the same employer. Where the employer has more than one establishment, the obligation will apply to the entire undertaking, rather than just one particular establishment.

Canadian women have long played a crucial role in scientific discovery. As we recognize their achievements, we must also look to the future. We must continue to encourage and support girls in the sciences, and help them to pursue their dreams and achieve their full potential.

the fact that Northern Ireland will continue to remain within the customs union. If that is the case, why has this been kept a secret from the British people?
I believe that the British people need to understand that leaving the European Union means that we will have a different relationship with the European Union than we currently have. The European Union has said that there will be no special deal for the United Kingdom. There will be no special deal for Northern Ireland.
And it is therefore a matter of fact, that the whole premise of the withdrawal agreement is the fact that Northern Ireland will remain within the customs union.
The withdrawal agreement, which has been negotiated with the European Union, reflects the fact that the UK has left the European Union.
The withdrawal agreement is about how we leave the European Union, and Northern Ireland is going to leave the European Union.
The future relationship, which is the second part of the UK’s relationship with the EU, will be negotiated after we leave the European Union.
And as part of that, the Northern Ireland Executive can propose that Northern Ireland should remain within the customs union.
It has to be a matter for the Northern Ireland Executive to decide, and the UK Government will support that.
The only way in which that can happen is if there is a special deal for Northern Ireland. Is that what you are suggesting?
I am not suggesting anything. What I am suggesting is that the European Union has said that there will be no special deal for the United Kingdom, and no special deal for Northern Ireland.
And therefore the premise of the withdrawal agreement is that Northern Ireland will leave the European Union, and that means that it will leave the customs union.
It is therefore a matter for the Northern Ireland Executive to decide whether Northern Ireland should remain within the customs union, and if that is what they decide to do, the UK Government will support that.
But is that not a special deal for Northern Ireland? Because we know that the UK, as a whole, has not negotiated any special deal.
