What is the Government’s definition of a booster shot? Is the Government using the word booster as a synonym for third dose? If so, what is the scientific rationale behind that decision?
There is a wealth of data on the effectiveness of a third dose, not just from the United Kingdom but from Israel and the United States. There is also data on the waning of immunity. I want to make sure that the Minister is aware of the concerns of the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) about waning immunity in the elderly. The UKHSA’s report on immunogenicity of the third dose of the vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, published on 21 September 2021, stated:
“Preliminary data from the UK Health Security Agency suggest that immunogenicity wanes faster in older adults with increasing age…in individuals over 80 years of age, the percentage of individuals with a significant decrease in neutralising antibodies after two doses of the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine is estimated to be 55%.”
The UKHSA’s report is a stark reminder that we need to protect the most vulnerable in our society, and we cannot afford to wait until the end of October to roll out the booster shots. I ask the Minister to bring forward her plans to implement a phased roll-out of the booster shots. I also urge the Minister to prioritise the elderly and vulnerable and to implement a phased roll-out of the booster shots alongside the roll-out of vaccines for children aged 12 to 15.

It is with great sadness that I rise in the House today to bring attention to this issue. I would like to pay tribute to the life of David Jeddore, a 20-year-old young man who was living in Happy Valley-Goose Bay at the time of his death.
I was inspired to speak in the House today because of a letter that I recently received from Mr. Jeddore's aunt, which included a message from David's mother, Loretta, who expressed her gratitude for my work on this issue.
David was a young man who was dealing with the challenges of being a young man. He was a young man who, like many young people in Happy Valley-Goose Bay and across the country, was struggling with the mental health challenges we hear so much about today. David was a young man who took his own life. His death was not in vain. David is not forgotten. He is a hero in his community and a hero in the province.
The sad fact is that we are losing too many young people to suicide. On average, 11 young people per day take their lives. One young person's suicide is one too many.
The fact that one in five young people will experience a mental health challenge is not acceptable. What is even more distressing is that when a young person does experience mental health challenges, there are not enough services or supports in place to help them.
That is why I am introducing a private member's bill in the House today. Bill C-238 , an act to amend the National Anthem Act (gender), would add the words “in all of us” to the line “in all of us command”. It would amend the gendered language in the national anthem to reflect the equality that exists in Canada.

Many of the stories relate to the same sort of problems that we see with the builders here at the CAB – but with a few extra, and rather more, nasty twists.
All too often the victims of cowboy builders are not only left with an unfinished job, but they are also left with a financial problem. We have seen cases of builders who have taken the money but failed to provide the goods or to do the work and then have disappeared leaving people without the funds to pay the next builder to finish the job. Some builders have taken money from their victims, left the site and then sold the materials, or used the money to pay off other debts and left the victims to foot the bill for materials and labour. Some have even been left with a debt for the work done, and the bills for the materials and labour. In one of the cases we have seen the victim has had to pay for workmen to come in and finish off the work done by the cowboy builder so that the house can be occupied.
So what can you do if you are the victim of a cowboy builder? The CAB is the first port of call for many people with problems. Unfortunately, the CAB cannot help in all cases, but we can provide information on what to do and how to avoid this sort of problem happening to you in the first place. We have a wealth of information on the CAB website, and this is also available on the Money Advice Service website (www.moneyadviceservice.org.uk) where there is also an on-line tool that helps you decide whether you need the help of a CAB adviser or just need some information about how to solve your problem.

So it is perhaps not surprising that the Prime Minister has turned to the media for help. At the start of this year he called the editor of the Daily Mail, Paul Dacre, to ask him to talk to his Cabinet colleagues about their “lack of ambition”. It was clear that the Prime Minister was looking for some leadership from a sector that, on the whole, has been an enthusiastic supporter of him and his colleagues. There was a moment of real hope when George Osborne was able to make his case to the Daily Mail’s readers on the paper’s website. However, the problem was that the Prime Minister has not backed his Chancellor. The Prime Minister has failed to listen to the business voices on the need to continue to invest in research, innovation, education and skills, or to listen to the calls for the Government to stop cutting the budgets of our universities.
The Government’s “cut, cut, cut” policies have created a climate of fear and a loss of confidence. There is no certainty about the future. It is hard to run a business, to recruit staff, to invest in capital projects or to develop new products when there is no certainty. And it is even harder to do this when the Prime Minister attacks business leaders for making plans for the future.
The Prime Minister has no credibility as a leader of Britain. He has no understanding of the importance of Britain’s relationship with the European Union and the need to protect our interests. He has no understanding of the importance of Britain’s place in the world, nor the significance of our soft power. He has no vision for Britain’s future or how to make our economy grow. He does not understand the importance of investing in research and innovation. He is not fit to lead Britain.
